Bukele Launches Military Rescue Operation For Four Salvadoran Troops Kidnapped In Haiti

El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele launched a military operation to rescue four Salvadoran aviation technicians kidnapped in conflict-ridden Haiti, warning gang leaders of more forceful action unless the Salvadorans are returned unharmed.

"Our kidnapped men are not combatants. They are aviation technicians who are part of our mission in Haiti, within the framework of an international mission. Our mission consists only of pilots and technical personnel, whose primary job is to carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war," Bukele wrote on X.

The four Salvadorans disappeared after gangs attacked their armored vehicle on Sunday in the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets, Port-au-Prince. They fled the vehicle after it caught fire.

Bukele said, "That is why, today, we have launched a military operation to rescue them. We have a single objective: to bring our four compatriots back home alive, without any harm."

Bukele's warning to gangs:

However, I want you, the gang leaders, to understand one thing very clearly: today's attack is nothing compared to what is coming if we do not get all four hostages back alive. And do not take our word for empty threats. We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too.

Pou chèf gang yo ak manm gang yo k ap kenbe kat konpatriyòt nou yo an otaj ann Ayiti: Mesye nou kidnape yo pa konbatan. Yo se teknisyen nan domèn avyasyon ki fè pati misyon nou ann Ayiti, nan kad yon misyon entènasyonal. Misyon nou an gen sèlman pilòt ak pèsonèl teknik, ki gen kòm travay prensipal fè evakyasyon medikal epi sove lavi moun, pa fè lagè. Men, nou te kidnape yo yon fason lach pandan yo t ap retounen apre yo te fin achte manje nan yon makèt nan zòn nan. Se poutèt sa, jodi a nou te lanse yon operasyon militè pou pote yo sekou. Nou gen yon sèl objektif: fè kat konpatriyòt nou yo retounen lakay yo vivan, san okenn mal. Men, mwen vle pou nou menm, chèf gang yo, konprann yon bagay byen klè: atak jodi a pa anyen devan sa k ap vini si nou pa remèt toule kat otaj yo vivan. Epi pa pran pawòl nou yo pou menas san fondman. Nou deja fini ak gang yo nan El Salvador, e nou kapab fini ak nou tou. Nou toujou gen tan pou evite sa. Haiti's government issued a press release late Wednesday saying the "abduction" of the four Salvadorans was an "absolute priority."

No group has claimed responsibility for the attack and subsequent abduction, which come as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade.

El Salvador, Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala are among the countries contributing to an international gang suppression mission that has more than 2,000 troops deployed in Haiti. title: Florida Mayor Charged With Grand Theft From COVID Relief Program She Helped Create
desc:
Florida Mayor Charged With Grand Theft From COVID Relief Program She Helped Create

Authored by Jill McLaughlin via The Epoch Times,

State authorities arrested the mayor of the central Florida city of Kissimmee on Oct. 21, charging her with grand theft and organized fraud over funds she received from a COVID-19 relief program.

Kissimmee Mayor Jackie Espinosa maintains her innocence after state charges were filed Oct. 21, 2026, accusing her of grant theft and organized fraud. Osceola County Jail

State Attorney General James Uthmeier accused Mayor Jackie Espinosa of illegally granting herself, her husband, and family members $50,000 from a city program she created that was meant to boost small businesses recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic.

Espinosa created, funded, expanded, and promoted the Kissimmee Business Boost 2.0 for small businesses and submitted her applications before anyone else on the first day it opened, which prosecutors alleged violated state law.

"The evidence makes very clear there was intent to engage in this conflict of interest, then ultimately abused her office to enrich herself," Uthmeier said during a press conference Wednesday.

The mayor and her family own several local businesses, including the Adanse, Real Estate Gallery, Matador Tacos and Tapas, and Empresas Espinosa. At the time of the applications, they also owned Kissimmee Diner.

Espinosa was handcuffed outside her home and taken to the Osceola County Jail, where she remained on Wednesday afternoon, according to jail records.

She is charged with one count of grand theft and one count of defrauding to obtain property, first- and second-degree felonies, according to Uthmeier.

Espinosa maintains her innocence, her lawyer Migdalia Perez told The Epoch Times.

"This case involves a publicly approved grant program administered by city staff, not a secret scheme to steal taxpayer money," Perez said in an emailed statement.

"The prosecution must establish that the mayor acted with criminal intent. We firmly maintain that she did not.

"There is a fundamental difference between an alleged ethics violation and a criminal offense," Perez added. "The state cannot transform one into the other without proving every element of a crime beyond a reasonable doubt."

Espinosa, who was elected as mayor in 2024, plans to challenge the allegations in court, her attorney said.

A state financial audit of the city's pandemic funding was performed as a routine matter, according to Florida's Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia, who oversees the state's financial services.

Auditors noticed irregularities in the city's Boost program, Ingoglia said, with funds allegedly linked directly and indirectly to the mayor.

"This led my team to look further," Ingoglia said.

During the investigation, auditors say they were allegedly told that some people in the city office attempted to ask Espinosa if her applications represented a conflict of interest, but they didn't get a response, Ingoglia said.

The city manager also allegedly notified her in a text message that the city attorney believed she was prohibited from receiving the grant funds, according to the arrest record.

Espinosa allegedly told the city manager she received the city attorney's opinion but "felt it was confusing," the court document stated.

Florida state law does not allow defendants to avoid criminal liability by claiming to not know they were violating the law, according to prosecutors.

The audit found three applications signed by Espinosa and filed before all other applications the day the funds became available, according to Ingoglia.

A couple walks in front of a house in Kissimmee, Fla., on Jan. 11, 2023. Marco Bello/Reuters

Of those, one company, Adanse LLC, which Espinosa legally retains 100 percent ownership of, received $20,000 in relief funds.

Her husband's company received $15,000 in funds, the audit found.

Ingolia said he and his team were with law enforcement when they arrested the mayor at her home in Tallahassee on Wednesday morning.

"I am proud of the outstanding work that my auditing team and Criminal Investigations Division did to uncover the alleged misuse of taxpayer dollars and to ensure that Jackie Espinosa's corruption did not go without recourse," Ingoglia said in a social media post.

A state ethics probe found Espinosa violated three ethics rules in July, which prompted the city commission to hold an impeachment vote against her.

The vote stalled after the commission deadlocked last month.

City commissioners also hired a special prosecutor to oversee the ethics complaint.

Espinosa faces up to 30 years in prison if convicted on all charges. A bond amount had not been set.

The city of Kissimmee said there had been no effects on its operations from the mayor's ordeal and regular business has continued.

"The city is prepared to follow the process outlined in the City Charter if a suspension occurs," Spokesperson Alibeth Suarez told The Epoch Times in an email.

"There are no impacts to city operations, which continue under the leadership of the City Manager and within the City's Council-Manager form of government."

title: UN Says 8,513 Casualties In Yemen Since August, Over 250K Displaced
desc:
UN Says 8,513 Casualties In Yemen Since August, Over 250K Displaced

There are new, grim numbers out of Yemen, after fierce fighting has been raging for many weeks going back to late August renewed war between the Saudi coalition (and its government in Aden), and the Iran-aligned Houthis.

The UN's World Health Organization on Thursday announced its tally of at least 8,513 casualties in the Yemen conflict since August. This is as of Oct.19, the WHO indicated.

According to the breakdown, this included 1,574 fatalities, and 6,939 others injured and wounded. The organization did not specify whether these were civilians or military personnel.

The WHO indicated further that over just the last eight-day period (counting backward from Oct.19), 292 people were killed and 1,048 others were injured.

Civilians have certainly borne a huge brunt of the renewed conflict, also with attacks spilling over into Saudi territory - where over 20 civilians have died, and cities and airports and energy sites have been targeted.

Al Jazeera reported earlier this week that at least a quarter-million people in Yemen have been displaced, which includes populations on both sides of the fighting.

"More than 250,000 people have been internally displaced in Yemen since the country’s war reignited in July, the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) has said, as fighting between Houthi rebels and forces loyal to the internationally recognized government rages across several fronts," the report said.

"The city of Taiz in southwestern Yemen is at the center of the displacement crisis, accounting for 76 percent of departures and hosting 52 percent of those newly displaced, UNHCR said in a statement on Tuesday," it added.

Additionally, according to the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR), "about 33,700 families still require shelter assistance amid severe underfunding of the humanitarian response to the war."

Nearly 260,000 Displaced by Fighting in #Yemen Since August, UN Says Nearly 260,000 people have fled their homes in Yemen since fighting escalated in August, with almost half seeking refuge in #Taiz Governorate, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said. The UN Human Rights Office has verified 57 civilian deaths and 194 injuries. Children accounted for half of those killed. Humanitarian partners have provided food, hygiene kits and emergency cash to more than 174,000 displaced people despite difficult operating conditions. Newly displaced families cited shelter as their most urgent need, followed by food and cash assistance. OCHA called on all parties to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, uphold international humanitarian law and allow the safe and sustained passage of aid and essential commercial goods into and across Taiz.

— Yemen Newsroom (@yemen_newsroom) October 22, 2026

The region has experienced on-and-off outbreaks of war and fighting going all the way back to 2014, when the Saudi-backed government began losing ground to the popular Houthi rebels. At one point the US was much more directly assisting the Saudi air campaign, but currently is said to only be playing an intelligence and advisory role.

Saudi coalition airstrikes have also gone back years, and the new outbreak of fighting has seen hundreds of air raids, which are especially devastating for civilians particularly in urban centers. The Houthis have in turn pummeled Saudi coalition areas with missiles and drones, which have also more frequently been sent across the border into the kingdom itself.

desc:

Via The Cradle

US special envoy Tom Barrack conceded that a "ground kinetic" battle in Yemen by the US "seems fruitless" during a talk at the Global Security Forum in Qatar on Tuesday.

"I think the president’s been clear that he supports Saudi Arabia and the backing that they need logistically he will supply. But America getting involved in a ground kinetic battle somewhere else seems fruitless." Barrack is Washington’s ambassador to Turkiye and special presidential envoy for Syria and Iraq.

He admitted that military force has failed in Yemen and that Riyadh is in a "very difficult position."

"These kinetic reactions have never worked. It doesn't work. It’s probably not likely that it’s going to work," he said.

Barrack questioned whether US meddling across West Asia has helped or harmed the region, arguing that Ansarallah in Yemen, Hezbollah in Lebanon, and the resistance factions in Iraq would lose their reason to exist only once states took responsibility themselves.

He pressed for talks between Riyadh, Sanaa, and regional mediators, urging regional capitals to build their own alliances instead of leaning on Washington.

He went further, admitting that the US has had a hand in 23 regime changes across the region, none of which achieved their aims.

He declined to say whether the US-Israeli war on Iran launched on February 28 was a mistake, while conceding that it had unleashed unintended consequences across the region.

The admission comes as the Saudi-led coalition presses on with airstrikes on Yemen, drawing retaliatory missile and drone strikes by the Yemeni Armed Forces (YAF) on the kingdom.

title: "Everyone Has Blown Up": London Macro Traders Carried-Out As French Carry Trade Implodes (Again)
desc:
"Everyone Has Blown Up": London Macro Traders Carried-Out As French Carry Trade Implodes (Again)

For the better part of three years, the hottest seat in London's multi-manager world was a European rates book: lever up French OATs in repo, clip the carry, collect the seven-figure payout. This month, the French bond market sent the bill.

According to a must-read report from eFinancialCareers' Sarah Butcher, London's macro hedge funds are quietly emptying out their EGB desks. Funds aren't talking about performance, but headhunters and bank traders who have been keeping score say the count of ejected European rates PMs and traders has climbed from the mid-70s a few weeks ago to close to 100 people. One senior trader at a liquidity provider summed it up in four words: "Everyone has blown up... they are all out"

In other words, the most crowded trade in European fixed income just found out what happens when the collateral is the problem.

And the bleeding hasn't stopped. This morning Bloomberg flashed that the French bond risk gauge is nearing 160bps, a fresh 15-year high, while French 10Y yields hit 5% for the first time since July 2002.

Below we walk through what blew up, why it blew up (twice), what Goldman, Morgan Stanley and the rest of the Street make of it, and why the market's attention is already drifting to the next domino: Italy.

The Trade: Borrow Against France, Pocket The Difference

The mechanics were simple enough to fit on a Post-it. Funds bought French government bonds, financed them in the repo market using those same OATs as collateral, and pocketed the gap between the bond's yield and the repo cost. Lever it up enough times and a few basis points of carry becomes a career. Per eFC, as French yields rose amid political chaos, OATs sold off and the whole highly leveraged structure was turned upside down.

A bank trader watching from the sidelines was less charitable:

"These people weren't even real portfolio managers," claims one senior trader, watching from the sidelines in a London bank.

"They were just using EGBs as a carry asset. Buying bonds, sitting on the carry and getting a percentage cut. It was fun for a while. You had a lot of PMs who were long France and long Italy, but with inflation coming in and rates high, it wasn't going to last."

Another PM in the sector offered a more philosophical take: "every bubble gets its moment."

The wider version of the trade, as Bloomberg reported on Oct 2, was the OAT asset-swap: funds such as Balyasny had built positions to harvest the spread between French yields and interest-rate swaps. Those were lucrative right up until the budget blowup of Oct 1, when the trades flipped from winners to liabilities and everyone hit the exit at once. RBC BlueBay's Kaspar Hense told Bloomberg what that looked like from the inside:

"Most typical hedge-fund strategies are in risk reduction mode. There have also been stop-loss levels triggered, partly on the steepener trades and now on long France trades." (emphasis ours)
— Kaspar Hense, RBC BlueBay Asset Management, via Bloomberg

Fidelity International's fixed income CIO Marion Le Morhedec went further, estimating that hedge fund activity could explain roughly half of the recent moves in the French-German spread, pointing to particularly heavy Eurex activity. Turns out the "liquidity providers" were also the liquidity takers.

Regular readers will recall that we called this one in real time on the very first day of the month:

it's been a while since we had a European sovereign debt crisis

*FRANCE-GERMANY 10-YEAR YIELD SPREAD WIDENS 8BPS TO 135BPS

France CDS widest in 13 years

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 1, 2026

...which was followed hours later by "Debt Crisis Back? European Bond Markets Crash, CDS Explode Amid France Budget Panic Contagion" (Oct 1). By the next day, the OAT-Bund spread hit 154bps, the widest since 2011, and the deleveraging was in full swing.

Same Trade, Same Crowd, Same Exit Door

The most damning detail in the eFC piece: according to the liquidity-provider trader, many of the PMs who blew up this month had already blown up in March, on the same positions. That was when the Iran war and the Hormuz shock triggered the first great European rates unwind, and when, per Bloomberg, multi-strats from Millennium to Balyasny to ExodusPoint gave back some or all of their year-to-date gains as crowded trades unwound.

Seven months apart, the same book got carried out twice. Diversification at its finest.

"They've blown up twice on the same trades."

Another trader observes that a lot of funds moved into the European fixed income space in the belief that it was easy money:

"The whole European carry system is now being questioned."

You can see both episodes in Goldman's own long-OAT/short-Bund rolling futures basket, which the bank's Systematic Trading Strategies desk circulated to clients: a steady grind higher for three years, a wobble in March, and then a near-vertical collapse that has wiped out roughly five years of gains as the basket fell from a February peak of ~104.3 to ~99.2.

Goldman's STS desk described the October contagion mechanism in that same note (available to pro subs here):

OATs have come roaring back into market focus over the last month. Where an unwind of popular rates positions following the latest ECB meeting (mostly steepeners), seemed to spread to wider carry trades in the rates space among a bid for volatility. A weak starting position for France with regards to debt and fiscal background and uncertainty into next year's election as well as challenging budget process didn't help. (emphasis ours)
— Goldman Sachs STS, Tim Huiszoon, Oct 12

Translation: the steepener crowd got stopped out first, then the losses bled into every other levered carry position on the same risk books. Not a fundamental repricing so much as a margin call with a French accent.

Allianz Trade agrees, noting in an Oct 9 report that speculative shorts, hedge-fund asset-swap unwinds and thin liquidity created a negative loop, with market depth more than 50% below normal:

"The speed reflects a positioning shock, not a pure repricing of fundamentals. Long-term investors are sitting out ahead of the elections... Fragmentation is far from 2012 or 2020 levels, but the ingredients are in place." (emphasis ours)
— Allianz Trade, "Toasted, not burnt", Oct 9

Note the second sentence: the real money that would normally buy the dip is sitting on its hands until the election. Which leaves... nobody.

The Plumbing Problem Nobody Wanted To Talk About

It's not just about P&L. Hedge funds have stepped in as the marginal provider of liquidity in European sovereigns precisely as central banks, pensions and banks stepped back. Per Bank of France data cited by Reuters, French government debt accounts for roughly €100 billion of the €250 billion in euro-area sovereign bonds pledged as repo collateral. In other words, France is the euro repo market.

So far the repo market itself has held up, but the risk is obvious: a further ratings cut narrows the pool of institutions able (or willing) to take OATs as collateral, which raises funding costs, which forces more selling. Commerzbank flagged exactly this back in September after Fitch's downgrade:

"...once a second agency downgrades to single-A, OAT repos may cheapen visibly, similar to BTPs, where more than half of bonds already trade above the depo rate." (emphasis ours)
— Commerzbank, via MNI, Sep 16

With Moody's reviewing France on Friday, that is not exactly a theoretical concern. And as we noted when the sell-side spent a day insisting the OAT rout was "just positioning," the contagion had already jumped to the banks, with the selloff reactivating Europe's "doom loop" (Oct 7). Goldman's European financials desk is still hiding under the desk:

"We are staying in risk off mode on banks (topics remains Euro sovereign crisis fear + Rates + Competition + Agentic, ie peak ROTE)... Appetite for French banks is very low given how long it will take to have some clarity." (emphasis ours)
— Goldman Sachs EU Financials specialist sales, Oct 20

"Overshot Fundamentals"... Says Goldman (Two Weeks Ago)

To be fair to Goldman, the bank has been leaning against the panic. Its strategists argued earlier this month that the OAT selloff appeared to have overshot fundamentals, amplified by positioning, though they conceded France is cheap relative to peers but lacks a catalyst. GS's STS desk went further on Oct 12, flagging GIR's expectation that the spread stabilizes at tighter levels and pitching a 1-year principal-protected option on OATs vs Bunds as a reversal trade with the 10Y spread at ~135bps.

The market had other plans. After weekend riots across France (nearly 2,400 arrests), the spread widened another 8bps to ~145bps on Monday, per Goldman's Daily Monitor, which ran this as its chart of the day: the OAT-Bund spread (inverted) dragging the euro down with it.

Goldman's FX desk confirmed the hedge funds were already heading for the exits:

"EUR option volumes – which have been an key indicator for broader portfolio hedges – have also decreased and are more than 30% off the highs. Certainly, a lot of hedges have been put on already and broad de-risking across popular positions was a hallmark of last week's activity." (emphasis ours)
— Goldman Sachs FX desk, Oct 19

Bloomberg's Vassilis Karamanis reads the same options market more darkly: the premium for longer-dated euro downside now exceeds short-dated, suggesting the euro's weakness "reflects more than a positioning adjustment." So much for "just positioning."

By Monday's close, French 10Y yields had posted their highest close since 2002 (Oct 20), and on Tuesday the spread hit a 156bps peak:

French bonds getting smashed: OAT-Bund spread back to crisis wides.

Expect ECB monetization demands to return

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 20, 2026

And this morning the milestone everyone was waiting for finally printed: per Bloomberg, French 10Y yields hit 5% for the first time since July 2002, with the OAT-Bund spread out another 5bps to 158bps as Brent traded above $110. So much for stabilizing at tighter levels.

Goldman's own economists, meanwhile, aren't buying the government's numbers either. In Tuesday's European Daily, Alexandre Stott writes:

"Recent protests over school underfunding and cost-of-living pressures have been among the largest since the pension reform strikes of 2019 and 2023 and the 'yellow vests' movement of 2018... we remain sceptical that the government will meet its deficit target of 5.0% of GDP next year... Our poll-based model therefore continues to see Le Pen as the clear favourite to become President next year." (emphasis ours)
— Goldman Sachs, European Daily: France—Budget Adoption Likely Later This Year, Oct 20

Morgan Stanley's chief global economist Seth Carpenter, whose note we published on Oct 11, is just as blunt about the arithmetic, and about the cavalry:

At wider than 150bps, the 30yr OAT-Bund spread surpassed the 130bp mark reached in the euro area debt crisis a decade ago... Debt stabilization would require a primary surplus of roughly 2% of GDP, a turnaround of about 5 percentage points. That shift would be larger than the adjustment required in Italy in the early 2010s... We think the bar for direct ECB intervention is very high, but France may not be the last test. (emphasis ours)
— Morgan Stanley, Seth Carpenter, Sunday Start

Put differently: the ECB is not coming to rescue anyone's carry book, and certainly not before Paris finds a fiscal squeeze bigger than the one Rome needed in 2011. Good luck with that during riots. Bill Blain, for his part, awarded a "No Sh*t Sherlock" prize to anyone who spotted European yields spiking after the riots, warning in Tuesday's Morning Porridge that the unrest could "metastasise into a potential bond crisis unless the ECB can swiftly demonstrate it is able, willing and stands ready to intervene."

Where Do 100 Ejected Rates Traders Go?

The career fallout is where the eFC report gets really fun. Some will drift back to the banks, where one headhunter said dealers need them to manage ECB exposure and bond books. The catch, per a bank trader: these PMs were pulling in $1 million-plus, a number that at a bank you only see as a desk head. Many are also tied up in non-competes, and some are still collecting guarantees and in no rush to find work. Good news for the departed PMs; allocators may see it differently.

Not everyone was pushed: one source estimated roughly 10% left voluntarily, some to raise their own funds, because allocators are struggling to find people both willing and able to take risk. Which is one way of describing a market where everyone who took risk just got carried out.

More ominous is the verdict from the trading floors: one trader told eFC that funds piled into European fixed income believing it was easy money, and that the whole European carry system is now being questioned. A bank trader called it systemic. And per the headhunter, the big fear now is that Italian BTP spreads go the way of OATs, a risk Morgan Stanley also flags, noting that wider OAT spreads are already putting pressure on BTPs.

Bottom Line

Goldman's bet is that this was a positioning flush: the levered carry crowd got shaken out, the forced selling is largely done, and spreads should drift back in. Maybe. But consider what has happened since the "overshoot" call: riots, a 5% 10Y, a spread nearing 160bps, a Moody's review on Friday, and a presidential race where Le Pen polls at 34%-38% in the first round. The forced sellers may be gone, but the natural buyers never came back, and the marginal bid in OATs for the past three years was a levered London pod that is now on gardening leave.

And this was never just about politics. Since the Hormuz crisis began, France has underperformed every major bond market, Italy included:

Which is why we lean toward the skeptics: this isn't the end of a positioning unwind, it's the beginning of a regime where France trades like the periphery, and where Italy, with the same crowd long it on the same leverage, is next in line. When the people who spent three years harvesting European carry are now warning that the asset class may never look the same, it's probably worth listening. Expect the ECB monetization chorus to get a lot louder. We'll check back after Friday's Moody's decision.

Much more in the full Goldman GS European Daily "France - Budget Adoption Likely Later This Year" note, both available to pro subs.

title: October Election Surprise Season Is Here!
desc:
October Election Surprise Season Is Here!

Authored by Ed Dowd: Beyond the Narrative via Substack,

October Surprise Season is back, right on schedule. The phenomenon is simple and well documented. Basically in the final weeks before a high-stakes election, an event, leak, crisis, or carefully timed disclosure appears that is meant to shift momentum, freeze the narrative, or force voters to reassess. The classic modern example remains 1980, when the Iran hostage crisis and the fear of a last minute Carter breakthrough gave the phrase its name. Bill Casey, running Reagan's campaign, used the term explicitly.

Decades later the pattern repeats with variations:

  • · George W. Bush's 1976 DUI surfacing days before the 2000 election

  • · The Trump Access Hollywood tape and the late Clinton email revelations in 2016

  • · Hurricane Sandy in October 2012 and Obama's response was positive for his campaign

  • · Assorted foreign policy or scandal drops that dominate cable and social media for 72 hours

The common thread is timing. With early voting, mail-in ballots, and compressed news cycles, an October event has maximum leverage and minimal time for full scrutiny or counter narratives. Whether organic or engineered, the incentives favor dramatic movement right before ballots are finalized.

Informal X Poll

On Tuesday October 20th I asked my X followers a direct question: two weeks until the midterms, so what will be the October surprise? The replies clustered around a few themes. One high-engagement response noted that USAID had been gutted and therefore "no money for surprises this year." I found that response quite humorous.

Another leaned toward nothing at all, arguing that the institutional interests prefer a blue team outcome so certain legislation (amnesty, digital ID, conscription) can pass with Trump's signature and the political blame can be shared...essentially a uniparty viewpoint.

A third predicted an Iran war escalation paired with a stock-market crash. Cyberattack scenarios, grid disruptions, and stock market rug-pulls also appeared repeatedly.

A forth expressed the feeling among many that you could post almost any absurd answer and it would seem plausible...a sign of the times.

The distribution was telling as relatively few expected a classic personal scandal or policy announcement that would clearly favor one side. More people expected either controlled chaos or deliberate inaction designed to produce a specific legislative or institutional result.

Well Timed NSA Cyber Security Alert

Yesterday the NSA issued a rare public cyber security alert. Organizations running PHP, the language powering an estimated 70 percent of websites, were told to prepare for updates addressing two critical vulnerabilities or take systems offline until mitigated. The flaws, reportedly identified with the assistance of frontier AI models from OpenAI's Patch the Planet effort and independently by Wiz, can provide a direct path to a server's file system or database. OpenAI described the issue as one of the most impactful in recent memory; patches were released the same day, and multiple governments echoed the urgency. The alert itself is legitimate on its face as PHP is foundational infrastructure. The timing is what stands out. Midterms are thirteen days away. Election administration, poll-book systems, voter-registration portals, and related state and local web applications are not immune to the same underlying technology stack. If unpatched or poorly patched systems are present in any voting-related infrastructure, the window for exploitation is now open. Even if the immediate risk is limited, the episode supplies a ready-made explanation for later anomalies: "cyber incident," "system offline for security," "delayed tabulation." History shows that once such an explanation exists, institutional actors have strong incentives to use it.

Potential Positive Trump Administration Surprises

Positive surprises for the incumbent side are also possible and would follow the same October logic. A credible framework that ends or freezes the Ukraine conflict, or a de-escalation agreement with Iran that reopens the Strait of Hormuz and stabilizes energy prices, would be classic late election cycle good news. Both theaters have already produced significant market and political volatility. A sudden diplomatic breakthrough that can be framed as "peace through strength" would dominate coverage, potentially shift polling among independents, and complicate Democratic messaging on foreign policy and inflation. Whether such deals materialize depends on counterparties who do not answer to U.S. election calendars, but the political incentive to announce progress is obvious and well understood by every administration.

Bottom Line: Post-Election Day Questions May Be The Surprise

The more durable issue, however, sits after Election Day. Mail-in and early voting volumes remain elevated in key jurisdictions. Statistical anomalies in the timing and distribution of ballots have been documented in prior cycles and have not been fully resolved to the satisfaction of large segments of the electorate. Chain-of-custody gaps, observer access limitations, and the continued use of systems whose source code and operational procedures are not fully transparent create legitimate questions about final tallies. I personally believe the system is broken and not secure from fraud. A cyber alert thirteen days out does not resolve those questions rather it potentially expands the set of post-election explanations available to whichever side loses. In that environment, the legitimacy of the reported results and the willingness of institutions and the public to accept them will matter more than whatever headline arrives between now and November 3. The October surprise, if it comes, will be noisy. The quieter and more consequential question is whether the post-election count can be shown, with evidence, to reflect the actual votes cast. That standard has not been consistently met in recent cycles, and the current technical and procedural environment does not make it more likely. Post election mayhem is my personal odds-on favorite.

title: Major US Banks Are Detecting Unauthorized AI Agents Accessing Customer Accounts
desc:
Major US Banks Are Detecting Unauthorized AI Agents Accessing Customer Accounts

America’s largest banks are scrambling to defend themselves against a new and rapidly evolving security threat: artificial intelligence agents gaining access to customer accounts, sometimes behaving in ways that appear to go beyond what their human users originally authorized, according to Axios.

Major financial institutions including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Morgan Stanley, Wells Fargo and Citigroup are confronting the growing presence of third-party AI assistants inside their banking platforms. Some institutions have detected unauthorized agent activity, while others are concerned about cases in which AI systems appear to initiate actions without explicit instructions from account holders.

The problem is becoming particularly difficult because banks cannot always distinguish between a legitimate customer accessing an account, an AI assistant acting with that customer's permission, and a potentially rogue agent operating outside its intended authority.

In many cases, customers themselves are providing AI tools with their banking credentials so the software can perform financial tasks on their behalf. While those arrangements may be voluntary, they frequently violate bank policies requiring account holders to maintain control of their login information.

More troubling is what happens once an AI agent gains access. Depending on the permissions it has been given, an assistant could potentially initiate purchases, transfer money or perform other financial transactions. Bank executives are increasingly concerned about the possibility of these systems making consequential decisions without adequate human oversight.

The Axios report out Thursday morning reported instances of agents interacting with bank call centers, as well as activity suggesting that certain systems may have attempted to act independently of their users' instructions. The developments have prompted several Wall Street institutions to begin tightening access to their platforms.

Morgan Stanley has reportedly started blocking third-party AI agents, while JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citigroup have also moved to restrict their activities. A Chase spokesperson cautioned customers against sharing account usernames and passwords, while Morgan Stanley said it had not identified instances of rogue AI agents accessing its systems.

The industry is not necessarily opposed to AI-powered financial assistants altogether. In fact, many banks already permit limited, read-only access to customer information through authorized third-party applications, including budgeting and personal finance software.

That model could provide a compromise for AI agents, allowing them to analyze balances, review transactions and help customers manage their finances without granting them the authority to actually move money.

But even that distinction is becoming more complicated as AI systems grow increasingly autonomous.

Banking executives acknowledge that consumers will likely demand more sophisticated AI assistants capable of handling financial tasks in the future. The challenge is developing safeguards that allow those capabilities without exposing customers to unauthorized transactions, compromised accounts or unpredictable automated behavior.

Compounding the problem is the speed at which the technology is evolving. Even banks with enormous cybersecurity budgets and extensive experience protecting critical financial infrastructure are struggling to keep pace with new vulnerabilities.

Financial institutions are consequently investing not only in preventing unauthorized AI activity, but also in preparing for potential failures. According to Axios, some are developing contingency plans for rapidly securing accounts and restoring customer access following a serious AI-related security incident.

The broader concern is that AI agents are advancing faster than the systems designed to supervise them. And in an industry where a single unauthorized action can have immediate financial consequences, the distinction between an assistant following instructions and an autonomous system acting on its own is becoming an increasingly important security problem.

For Wall Street, the challenge is no longer simply figuring out how to incorporate artificial intelligence into banking. It's figuring out how to keep increasingly capable AI systems from doing things that neither the banks nor their customers intended.

Political polling guru Nate Silver unleashed a profanity-laced tirade after a polling operation admitted its surveys were largely fabricated.

Silver, whose career has been built around interpreting polling data, was furious after Wedgewood Polling admitted that much of its operation had been an elaborate "social experiment" designed to expose just how easily questionable statistics could infiltrate the political media ecosystem.

"Our fabricated numbers were given instant credibility across national media platforms," the statement said. "The ease with which unverified figures were absorbed into mainstream political narratives highlights a systemic breakdown in media vetting and data aggregation."

In an episode of the Still Counting podcast alongside Galen Druke and Clare Malone, Silver made his feelings abundantly clear.

"I say go fuck yourselves. I hope you're put in jail," Silver declared, before quickly clarifying that he did not mean the threat of imprisonment "literally."

Wedgewood's operators portrayed the stunt as an experiment highlighting weaknesses in modern political polling and journalism.

Yet, Silver was in no way amused.

"People on Twitter are sometimes too kind to these enterprising college kids or whatever they are that start doing these kind of polls that are even at best kind of mediocre," he complained.

The veteran election analyst acknowledged that deliberately distributing false information could still qualify as constitutionally protected speech, but suggested the operation might have exposed itself to legal problems by crowdfunding certain surveys.

"If you're doing these sort of narrative-setting polls then maybe you are buying positions on prediction markets and then the line goes up and you cash them out or whatever else... or you have a political agenda," Silver said.

Abdul El-Sayed's campaign even cited the group's fake polling during his primary battle against Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow and Rep. Haley Stevens, according to Fox News.

"These people are absolute scumbags," former Kamala Harris advisor Mike Nellis told Fox News. "They can try to claim that they have some moral high ground here, but they lied about their polling data, got caught, and are freaking out because they've committed fraud."

"The people responsible for this should be run out of American politics, and if they can be, they should be prosecuted to the full extent of the law," Nellis said. title: Sell The Bailout: Skydance Tumbles As Musk's $1 Billion Check Reminds Everyone Paramount Needs One
desc:
Sell The Bailout: Skydance Tumbles As Musk's $1 Billion Check Reminds Everyone Paramount Needs One

It took about ten minutes.

Just after noon on Thursday, Semafor reported that Elon Musk has invested roughly $1 billion in Skydance (SKYD), the newly renamed Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery combo run by David Ellison. The stock did what stocks are supposed to do on a billionaire endorsement and spiked to $8.46, up 7.5% on the day. Then traders actually thought about it, and by 12:10pm the shares had been halted for volatility after tumbling, before printing a low of $7.53 once trading resumed, 11% below the post-headline spike.

*SKYDANCE HALTED FOR VOLATILITY AFTER SHARES TURN NEGATIVE (narrator: "not up")

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 22, 2026

Our own read of the headline was about as succinct as it gets:

Market: "wait, Paramount needs a bailout?"

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 22, 2026

Which, well, is probably the right question. Because while equity investors had been hoping for a white knight, credit investors have spent the past three weeks pricing Skydance like a company that would very soon need one.

The CDS Market Already Knew

Regular readers know we have been all over the Skydance capital structure since the deal financing hit the tape. On October 1, we documented how Paramount's record $52 billion bond offering sank before the ink was dry, with the 8-year second-lien notes trading around 95 within a day of pricing at par, and 5Y CDS jumping to 432bp, the highest since April 2009. Five days later, as the Warner deal closed, Fitch sent the old Paramount unsecured paper to the back of the line behind ~$57 billion of new secured debt, and the legacy 6.875% 2036s plunged to a record low of 77 cents.

It was all downhill from there: Paramount CDS soared to Global Financial Crisis levels on October 7, took out the Lehman highs on October 14 and, on Tuesday night, we put out this chart showing 5Y CDS at a new all-time record of 601bp, comfortably above anything on record.

Put differently, the credit market has been screaming for weeks that Skydance has too much debt and not enough equity. So when the solution to that problem turned out to be a $1 billion check, it maybe shouldn't come as a surprise that equity holders reached the same conclusion as the CDS desks: if the company is raising emergency-sized equity from friends of the family, there must be an emergency.

Malone Promised $10 Billion. Musk Sent One

The other problem is that the market had been primed for a much bigger number. Just one day earlier, billionaire media mogul John Malone told the Paley International Council Summit that a Musk investment was coming, and that it would be big:

"Who helped Elon finance Twitter when he bought it? Larry Ellison. How did Larry Ellison come up with some of the money to put into the creation of Skydance? Tesla stock. And I would not doubt for a minute that before very long you're gonna see an announcement."

Malone was right about the announcement, but he pegged the check at $8 billion to $10 billion. Musk delivered about one-tenth of that. Against Skydance's roughly $87 billion of total debt, the Musk money comes to a little over 1%, or about the same weight as a rounding error in the company's synergy targets.

Some napkin math: the fixed-rate notes sold in the deal financing alone carry about $3.3 billion a year in coupons, and the ~$9.5 billion of term loans at SOFR+275 add maybe another $650 million. Call it $4 billion a year in interest on the acquisition debt, which means Musk's $1 billion covers roughly one quarter's worth of interest. Generous, sure. Transformational, not quite.

Per Semafor, the Musk money came in around the same time as fresh equity from Skydance's other investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs, though neither the size of those checks nor the price paid has been disclosed (and if the price had been flattering, we suspect someone would have mentioned it). Skydance declined to comment and Musk's camp didn't respond.

Who Needs The Money, Anyway?

None of this should be news to anyone who has followed the saga. When Semafor first reported back in September that Paramount was weighing tapping Musk for an equity check (Sep 24), the stated rationale was to "reduce Larry Ellison's financial burden" after the Oracle founder personally guaranteed more than $40 billion of the equity financing. Fitch, for its part, made it clear in its rating action timed to the close that hitting the company's 3x net leverage target by the end of 2029 would likely require issuing equity or selling assets on top of the promised $6 billion in cost cuts.

So here is the equity. A very small amount of it.

Meanwhile, the stock has been a one-way trip since the merger closed. Skydance ended October 6 at $9.53 and is now trading around $7.80, a drop of about 18% (some of that is the October 14 warrant distribution, which knocked 16% off the price as shares started trading ex-warrant, so the damage is less dramatic than it looks, but only a bit). That said, the real story is in credit, where the equity drawdown is a sideshow next to bonds at record lows and CDS above Lehman.

And there is one more wrinkle that we flagged when CDS first took out the 2008 highs: how much of this is effectively cross-collateralized with Larry Ellison and, by extension, Oracle (ORCL), whose own CDS was hitting record highs at the same time? With the Ellison family on the hook for a big chunk of Skydance's equity and Oracle's balance sheet already stretched by the AI capex binge, a little outside help is probably welcome. A little is what it got.

Friends With Benefits

Of course, there is more to the Musk check than finance. The world's richest man, who already owns X, now has a stake in the parent of CNN and CBS, and the Ellisons, via Oracle, are part owners of TikTok's US operations. Semafor's original September scoop was enough to cause panic at CNN; today's confirmation will probably do the same, even though David Ellison has insisted the newsrooms will stay editorially independent. Given how many times CNN has warned its viewers about Elon Musk, there is a certain poetry in Musk now being one of its shareholders.

Markets, however, trade the debt stack, and the debt stack says Skydance needs a lot more than $1 billion. If anything, today's tape suggests that each new "vote of confidence" will be read as a sign of how much more is needed, which is why we suspect this check is the first of several, and that the next one will have to be far closer to Malone's number than Musk's.

Until then, the CDS market will keep its own counsel. It hasn't been wrong yet.

title: Virginia Governor Seeks 6-Year Rate-Freeze If Dominion-NextEra Merger Is Approved
desc:
Virginia Governor Seeks 6-Year Rate-Freeze If Dominion-NextEra Merger Is Approved

By Charles Paullin of UtilityDive

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, D, has proposed a six-year rate freeze as part of a suite of conditions she says state regulators should impose if they approve a proposed merger between Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy that could create the largest regulated electric utility in the world.

Spanberger’s stance comes amid review of the $67 billion merger that has prompted intense pushback from other state officials and local communities.

“Any proposed merger involving Virginia’s primary state-regulated utility must benefit families, small businesses, and Virginia’s workforce — not just the shareholders of these multi-billion-dollar corporations,” Spanberger said in a statement Monday.

“That’s why I am calling for a six-year freeze to Virginians’ base residential electricity rates, a tripling of monthly bill credits for ratepayers, and additional commitments to lower energy costs and meet our long-term clean and homegrown energy goals if the State Corporation Commission is to approve this merger,” she added.

Expert witness testimony filed by Spanberger’s office with the State Corporation Commission outlined a plan to increase monthly bill credits to $29 a month for four years, as well as increasing the debt share of Dominion’s capital structure from 48% to 60% to lower its rate of return.

The witness, Richard McCann, an environmental consultant with M.Cubed, also called for requiring a “probability of dispatch” cost allocation method, improving disconnection policies and several other energy efficiency and clean energy commitments.

“Mandatory, Comprehensive Enforceability provisions must be imposed to hold the Joint Petitioners fully accountable for any violation of commitments, including the labor and workforce commitments,” wrote McCann. “Unless these additional commitments are substantially addressed or alternative solutions are identified, the Commission should reject the joint petition.”

The filings coincide with filings from Virginia’s attorney general and SCC staff opposing the deal unless terms they propose are also agreed to.

Dominion and NextEra proposed the merger in May, saying it would facilitate a more cost-effective buildout of Virginia’s electric grid to serve rising demand from large-load data centers.

The utilities initially proposed customer bill credits amounting to $10 a month for two years. But as pushback mounted, including from Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi, the utilities increased the proposed timeline to four years. The utilities also made assurances for more clean energy, in line with the state’s decarbonization law, the Virginia Clean Economy Act.

“As expected in a proceeding of this size and significance, today’s testimony reflects a wide range of viewpoints and interests,” Dominion and NextEra said in a joint statement following the governor’s announcement. “We are reviewing the filings and will address the issues raised through the Commission’s established process.”

Spanberger plans to hold a call with the media Tuesday afternoon to discuss her proposal.

“If companies want to make their Data Centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a ‘dividend,’” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Wednesday.

New data centers, which are required to fuel the growth of artificial intelligence (AI), have become politically controversial in some areas because of the amount of electricity and water they consume.

Local resistance blocked or delayed at least 75 data center projects, worth $130 billion, in the first quarter of 2026, according to Data Center Watch.

The Trump administration has supported AI, and the president said last month that U.S. government documents would start referring to it as “super intelligence.”

“As the President of the United States, I have been watching Data Centers very closely, and have come to a very strong conclusion,” Trump wrote on Wednesday.

“New and large, in some cases gigantic, Data Centers are mandated by me to make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid, and therefore there is [an] electric price increase. In fact, there could be a substantial decrease.”

‘Get Them Built’: Trump

“MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE U.S.A,” Trump also wrote.

The president said he supports “co-location” of new energy sources and data centers to accelerate AI infrastructure buildout through initiatives that fast-track permits, reduce regulatory hurdles, and make federal land available for these projects.

Meta has agreed to build a data center on the site of a planned 400-megawatt natural gas plant in New Albany, Ohio, and Google has partnered with Intersect Power to build co-located data centers in so-called energy parks alongside solar and storage generation in a nationwide $20 billion venture.

"Gotten Too Old Not To Be Greedy": Virginia State Sen. Arrested, Accused Of Masterminding $4.5 Million Criminal Drug Enterprise

Virginia's Democratic Senate President Pro Tempore L. Louise Lucas, 82, has been indicted by a federal grand jury and taken into federal custody on charges of racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute marijuana, money laundering, honest-services fraud/bribery, and maintaining a drug-involved premises. Six co-defendants, including her daughters and grandson, were also charged. FBI Director Kash Patel put the alleged scheme at roughly $4.5 million.

The 45-page indictment unsealed Thursday in the Eastern District of Virginia alleges that Lucas led a multi-year "Lucas Enterprise" that, since at least 2019, acquired and distributed at least 100 kilograms of illegal marijuana, laundered the proceeds through various business entities, and used her official power to protect the operation while shaping cannabis legislation for personal gain. Lucas self-surrendered Thursday morning and faces an initial appearance before a federal magistrate judge. All defendants are reported to be in custody.

Who She Is and How the Probe Unfolded

Lucas has represented Portsmouth since 1991 and has served as Senate President Pro Tempore and Chair of the Finance and Appropriations Committee - the most powerful budget post in the chamber. She is a longtime, outspoken advocate for marijuana legalization who sponsored key bills and co-owns The Cannabis Outlet, a Portsmouth shop that sells hemp and cannabis products. She is a close ally of Governor Abigail Spanberger and played a central role in Democrats' 2026 redistricting effort that sought to add Democratic-leaning congressional seats before it was blocked by the Virginia Supreme Court.

The case became public on May 6, 2026, when the FBI executed court-authorized search warrants at Lucas's Portsmouth district office (which also houses her disabilities-services business, Lucas Lodge LLC) and at The Cannabis Outlet next door. Agents recovered marijuana and firearms from both locations. At the time, Lucas publicly described the raids as political intimidation. Federal sources told Fox News the searches were part of a major corruption probe. The underlying investigation itself predates the current administration and was opened under President Biden. Wiretaps were active for months; at least one Democratic congressman and a local reporter later received notices that their communications with Lucas had been intercepted.

Via Wavy.com:

The response was described as “court-authorized law enforcement activity,” according to FBI Public Affairs Specialist Cassandra Temple. She could not offer additional information.

A spokesperson for the FBI later elaborated in the following statement to WAVY: “The FBI is executing a court-authorized federal search warrant in Portsmouth, VA. There is no threat to public safety. This is an ongoing investigation, and no further information is publicly available at this time.”

The Allegations

Prosecutors say Lucas directed the purchase and sale of large quantities of illegal marijuana under the cover of her licensed medical-cannabis business and used her legislative position to "insulate the enterprise from criminal scrutiny and influenc[e] legislation to financially benefit themselves."

A central allegation involves an August 2022 payment of $750,000 by Lucas for a 100% stake in a shell holding company created so a co-conspirator could obtain a Virginia recreational marijuana license. She allegedly failed to disclose this interest on required Statements of Economic Interests. She is also accused of receiving a bribery payment from the co-conspirator and of meeting with him at her Capitol office to discuss partial repayment while lobbying other legislators on the license.

Intercepted calls are explicit. In February 2026 Lucas told an unindicted co-conspirator this was their "last chance at generational wealth" and added, "I've gotten too old to not be greedy." In another call she reportedly said she needed the recreational market to open because "when I did it, it was obviously illegal." She had earlier told a co-conspirator she wanted a recreational license specifically "to create generational wealth for her and her family" and that "this is my last chance."

The Cannabis Outlet itself received violation notices from the Virginia Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services in 2023 and 2024 for selling non-compliant products.

Co-defendants include daughters Lisa Lucas-Burke and Theresa Lucas-Lamb, grandson Ryan Eichelberger, former business partner Carlton Upton Jr., Prince Albert William Hudson III, and Tameka Johnson.

Statements and Timing

Attorney General Todd Blanche said the charges "reveal the behavior of a public servant who will put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve." Patel stated that Lucas "allegedly abused her position of public trust as a 30-year Virginia State Senator to put her own financial interests ahead of the people she represents - orchestrating a five-year scheme worth an estimated $4.5 million."

In a statement, Lucas said: "Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother. I grew up under Jim Crow. I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I'm not stopping now."

Virginia recently cleared the path for regulated recreational retail sales beginning July 1, 2027. Lucas is not up for reelection until 2027. The charging decision comes roughly two weeks before midterm elections - an unusual window for overt action against a sitting political figure, though the investigation itself is not new.

title: US To Release Heating Oil Reserve In Northeast To Lower Prices
desc:
US To Release Heating Oil Reserve In Northeast To Lower Prices

Authored by Jack Phillips via The Epoch Times,

The U.S. Department of Energy has announced it will offer a heating oil exchange in a bid to lower costs ahead of the winter as the war in Iran continues.

In a statement released on Wednesday, the department announced a proposal request for an exchange of up to 315,000 barrels of ultra-low sulfur distillate, a refined oil product used for home heating. Ultra-low sulfur distillate uses the same specification as most types of diesel, which has experienced high prices in recent days.

"This solicitation is structured to mitigate supply chain challenges disrupting fuel oil supply," the department said, adding the move is designed to keep the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve stocked ahead of the winter months.

"The Trump administration is committed to doing everything in our power to lower energy costs for the American people," said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said in a statement.

According to the Energy Department, the terms of the exchange mean that borrowing companies have to "return the same volume of fuel oil" and include a premium back to the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve.

After receiving letters from the two Maine U.S. senators, Wright said he then directed his agency to exchange barrels of fuel from the oil reserve to mitigate high heating oil costs.

"Of course, this is a temporary measure to solve a temporary supply disruption. I encourage the governors of New York and New England to work with the Trump Administration to build the Constitution Pipeline and replace home heating oil with low-cost natural gas," he said. "Doing so would save their residents billions of dollars in home heating and electricity costs."

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) wrote in a post on X that the move equals a roughly 13 percent supply increase for New England, essentially pushing down the northeastern United States' heating oil costs this winter.

The Energy Department's announcement added that it will loan the hundreds of thousands of barrels of heating oil from Connecticut, Maine, and Massachusetts. The deliveries will be completed by Nov. 13.

According to the American Automobile Association (AAA), the average retail price of diesel has remained over $6 per gallon for weeks. From Tuesday to Wednesday, the price for diesel remained virtually unchanged in the United States, standing at $6.31 per gallon.

Diesel hit a record high of $6.52 per gallon on Sept. 22, the AAA figures show. Those figures also show that regular gasoline dropped about 1 cent on Wednesday to $4.26 per gallon.

Oil prices have hovered around $100 per barrel for months now, with international Brent crude reaching $108 and U.S. West Texas International reaching $97, respectively, per barrel on Wednesday.

In an effort to control crude oil prices that have risen due to the war with Iran and amid the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the Trump administration in March agreed to loan 172 million barrels of crude from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, located in Louisiana and Texas. Currently, the reserve has dropped to 282 million barrels, the lowest levels seen since the 1980s.

President Donald Trump also indicated that his administration may move to permanently allow E-15 gasoline, which is blended with 15 percent ethanol instead of the regular 10 percent, to be used all year long. Normally, some states bar its usage during the summer months.

During a rally in Kansas on Monday, Trump said he would initiate the move if Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) wins his reelection bid during the midterms next month.

title: CoreWe've Got Bills To Pay: Bernstein Sees $76 Billion Funding Hole At Imploding Neocloud
desc:
CoreWe've Got Bills To Pay: Bernstein Sees $76 Billion Funding Hole At Imploding Neocloud

Goldman's CoreWeave upgrade is three days old, and so far it has achieved precisely nothing.

On Monday, Goldman's Gabriela Borges upgraded CoreWeave (CRWV) to Buy (in the process cutting her price target by almost a quarter) which is a creative way to turn bullish:

On CRWV, Goldman was Neutral with a $139 price target. it is now a Buy with a $106 price target.

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 19, 2026

The stock spiked to $66 premarket and then, right after the open, gave back the entire pop, prompting us to note that Goldman was gonna need a bigger upgrade:

The opposite happened: a day later, HSBC tore apart Goldman's bull case a new one with a $39 target ("the more it invests, the more the value destruction"), and this morning it's Bernstein's turn. CoreWeave is down another 8% this morning to $56.70, below where it traded before Goldman said "Buy", and below the 52-week low of $57.24.

Goldman, meanwhile, doubled down. Late on Wednesday, Borges published a follow-up titled "How big is the funding gap?" (available to pro subs), because, in her words, "the primary question we have received from investors is around the magnitude and viability of future funding needs." Her answer: about $23 billion. Bernstein's answer, published a few hours later: $76 billion.

Somebody's math is off by more than three times. Let's figure out whose.

"Not Great, Not A Surprise"

Bernstein's Madison Rezaei, who correctly had an Underperform on CoreWeave since initiating seven months ago, cut her price target to $51 from $74 in a note with what is hands down the best title of the year: "Core-We've got bills to pay... lowering our PT" (also available to pro subs). She also cut her target EV/EBIT multiple to 23.5x from 25.5x, "primarily reflecting concerns around its cost of capital, especially as the company moves to shorter-dated contracts."

The note follows a week of what Rezaei describes as non-stop calls with "hedge funds, LOs, bulls, bears, credit people, REIT investors, and everybody in between." The first question on everyone's mind was the same one Goldman tried to answer, and Bernstein's reply is refreshingly blunt:

"Not great, not a surprise. We estimate CRWV needs to raise $85B to fund the existing committed backlog, $9B of which is already covered by existing facilities. The unsecured credit market are still open to them at rates in the 15%+ range, given where the bonds are trading today, but we think there are a range of more reasonable options."

In other words, $76 billion of fresh money just to deliver the compute CoreWeave has already sold, before signing a single new contract. And no, CoreWeave can't simply stop growing its way out of the problem. Bernstein specifically addresses the investors asking whether the company could just slow spending and harvest cash:

"We distinguish stopping new contract wins from stopping investment: even without additional backlog, the company would still need to fund deployment obligations embedded in existing contracts, as well as maintenance and replacement requirements. Even a no-additional-backlog scenario would not produce immediate improvements in profitability given the funding requirements of existing contracts."

Bernstein models roughly $46 billion of growth capex next year to deliver existing backlog plus about $6 billion of maintenance capex, for a total of $52.5 billion in 2027, actually above consensus. And even in the "no future backlog" scenario, 2027 capex is still $43.5 billion. The good news, if you want to call it that, is that Bernstein's capex falls off a cliff after 2027 because it is well below the Street on growth in 2028 and beyond. Bulls may not see it that way.

Bernstein also took an axe to earnings: its 2026 adjusted EPS loss widens to -$5.14 from -$4.56, and 2027 to -$6.81 from -$4.77, with adjusted losses persisting through at least 2029 in its model. That's three more years of losses on top of the $76 billion.

Goldman's $23 Billion Napkin

Now for Goldman's version. Borges walks through three illustrative scenarios, and the headline (as per the title of her one and only exhibit) is that debt needed to serve existing $129 billion backlog "could be $20-23bn when including customer prepayments," while ramping all 4.2GW of secured power would take about $38 billion.

Look a little closer at that table, though, and the number gets small mostly because of what goes into it. In Scenario 1, CoreWeave needs about $60 billion of capex to serve its backlog. Goldman assumes 80% can be debt-financed through DDTLs, subtracts $10.6 billion of committed-but-undrawn DDTL capacity and $10.4 billion of "cash optionality", and arrives at $36.7 billion of new debt. To get to the headline $22.9 billion, it then assumes customers hand over 20% of total contract value up front, or $15.7 billion. Stretch GPU useful life to six years, and the number shrinks further to $19.5 billion.

A few problems with that:

  • The prepayments are going the wrong way. By Goldman's own admission, "CoreWeave's prepayment percentages have come down in the last 6 months." Goldman's spin is that this "suggest[s] these percentages can also go up in an environment where there is less visibility into debt financing." Translation: when CoreWeave can't borrow, its customers will happily lend it the money instead. Maybe. Or maybe customers who just watched CoreWeave's bonds trade at 15% decide they'd rather not prepay a counterparty with distressed debt.
  • The "cash optionality" is optimistic. The $10.4 billion includes $2.2 billion from selling 35 million ATM shares at $64, about 9% above where the stock trades this morning, and a $2 billion revolver. According to Bernstein's debt table (as of Oct 20), $1.2 billion of the $2.5 billion revolver is already drawn, which would leave $1.3 billion.
  • The 4.2GW number needs $52.7 billion of customer money. Scenario 3's $38 billion assumes prepayments of $52.7 billion. Without them, the new debt needed is $84.5 billion, at a 94% debt-to-loan ratio, which is well above the 80% cap Goldman itself says the DDTL structure allows. Funny how that number didn't make the title.
  • There is no cost of capital anywhere in the note. Goldman calculates how much CoreWeave needs to borrow, but not at what rate, deferring to the "financing cost assumptions in our upgrade note" (the one with a 10% cost of new debt, about two-thirds of what CoreWeave's unsecured bonds currently yield).

Here is the full range of answers to "how much does CoreWeave still need to borrow", depending on whose spreadsheet you trust and what you assume customers will do:

To Goldman's credit, the note ends with "Our worksheet is available on request and we welcome feedback on our assumptions." Consider this our feedback.

Goldman's Model Disagrees With Goldman's Note

The irony is that the best rebuttal to Goldman's funding note can be found on page 2 of the very same note, in Goldman's own financial model. Ignore the illustrative scenarios and look at the cash flow statement, and Goldman has CoreWeave burning $28.2 billion of free cash flow in 2026, another $28.2 billion in 2027 and $15.8 billion in 2028, on capex of $38.6 billion, $48.0 billion and $49.9 billion. To fund that, Goldman's model has debt increasing by $26.7 billion this year, $26.6 billion in 2027 and $20.0 billion in 2028. That's $46.6 billion of new debt in the next two years alone, double the headline "funding gap", and that's before $50 billion of lease liabilities which Goldman models by 2028 (and which are, of course, debt by another name).

Long-term debt goes from $14.9 billion at the end of 2025 to $90.8 billion by 2028. Goldman's interest coverage ratio for CoreWeave is 0.3x this year and 0.7x in 2027, meaning operating profit doesn't even cover the interest bill until 2028, when it reaches a still-miserable 1.3x. Net debt to equity peaks at 3,059% in 2027. And cash on the balance sheet drops to $1.2 billion at the end of 2027, which is a little thin for a company with $6 billion in annual interest expense (also per Goldman).

Which brings us to the obligatory disclosure appendix, where Goldman notes it "is acting as a manager or co-manager of a pending underwriting" for CoreWeave, owns 1% or more of the stock, and expects "to receive or intends to seek compensation for investment banking services in the next 3 months." As we said on Tuesday, none of this makes the analysis right or wrong. But if CoreWeave really does need somewhere between $20 billion and $85 billion in new money, it's nice to know who'll be helping raise it (the same one, mind you, that just upgraded the stock).

15% Money And The DDTL Treadmill

Back to Bernstein, which does what Goldman doesn't: it looks at what the debt costs, when it comes due and who it sits with. CoreWeave has $42.1 billion of debt outstanding and a $3.3 billion annual interest bill, a blended rate of 7.8% that is dragged down by $10.8 billion of 2-3% converts. Everything else is priced like junk, because it is.

On Bernstein's numbers, CoreWeave's gross debt is 8.6x LTM adjusted EBITDA, or 11.7x on total committed capacity, and still 7.4x on next year's EBITDA:

The good news is that most of the debt matures in 2030-2032 (about $31 billion in those three years), so Bernstein does not "expect the company to see real distress anytime soon." The less good news is that the DDTLs are amortizing structures, and "principal repayments and covenant tests begin well before final maturity, making near-term debt service and covenant headroom important considerations."

How near-term? According to Bernstein's DDTL calendar, monthly repayments on DDTL 5.0 begin around October 22, 2026, i.e. today (CoreWeave says November), with the first 1.35x DSCR covenant test due around November 30. DDTL 5.5 starts amortizing in January, and the $8.5 billion DDTL 4.0 next July:

Then there's the cost of new money. CoreWeave's unsecured bonds yield around 15%, which Bernstein calls "an important signal of the market's required compensation for risk," and the most recent secured facility was hardly cheap either: DDTL 5.5, priced in August, came in at SOFR+5.50%, the widest spread since the very first DDTL in 2023. Bernstein thinks "subsequent deals could price even higher."

And here is the catch-22 at the heart of Bernstein's thesis. CoreWeave needs to move toward shorter contracts with enterprise customers to remain competitive with hyperscalers (who are also its biggest customers and are building their own capacity). Shorter contracts capture higher pricing per MW. But...

"Unfortunately those contracts are riskier to creditors and do not help CRWV lower its cost of capital. DDTL 5.5 was at SOFR+5.5% - this is the best proxy; subsequent deals could price even higher."

Put differently, the more CoreWeave does what it needs to do strategically, the more it costs to fund. Bernstein assigns "a low, nonzero probability" to CoreWeave building a sufficiently differentiated enterprise business, which is about as polite as sell-side prose gets.

A 9% Business With A 32% Story

Which brings us to returns. Bernstein runs the numbers on what it believes is CoreWeave's best contract, the Meta deal (including the $21 billion expansion), and gets a best-case unlevered IRR of 9-12% (9% in its illustrative model). Levered, it jumps to 32%, which sounds great until you look at how it gets there:

CoreWeave spends $10.8 billion of capex, borrows $10 billion of it, puts in $756 million of equity, and then collects... $129 million a year in levered free cash flow for five years, with the bulk of the return riding on a $2.3 billion residual value in year six. In other words, the 32% is almost entirely leverage plus a bet on what six-year-old GPUs will be worth in 2031. And that's on 9% unlevered returns, against new money that costs 9% secured and 15% unsecured. HSBC made the same point on Tuesday with its 8.9% ROIC, and Bernstein's math gets to the same place from a different direction.

Management says contracts signed since 2Q have "materially better economics." Bernstein's response is that the newer contracts "may be too small to change overall blended returns meaningfully," and its "view leans toward medium-term economics resembling the older contracts more closely."

Not A Zero... Just A Ward Of Jensen

To be fair to CoreWeave, Bernstein is not calling for a wipeout: "We do not believe CRWV is a 0 - they still have a large backlog, line of sight to powered shell delivery, and while we don't think the contracts are super attractive, they're not underwater." Prediction markets seem to agree, at least after SpaceX's blowout quarter:

stellar SPCX results sent Coreweave bankruptcy odds (by Dec 31, 2028) sharply lower https://t.co/Mjc8LU7xjp

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 21, 2026

The floor, in Bernstein's view, is the same one that has been debated on these pages since the meltdown began last week: Nvidia. Asked whether Jensen would step in, Bernstein says "we think they would intervene in a true downside. Doesn't necessarily re-energize the stock, but raises the floor." Which is great news for CoreWeave shareholders, if a little awkward for Huang, who told everyone last week that CoreWeave's cost of capital was "actually decreasing." Well, no... it's not of course, and as one of our contributors put it on Saturday, Jensen will blink first.

Bernstein's other conclusion is that the damage is "semi-contained": "If it ceased to exist tomorrow, colo contracts would be absorbed and the rest of the market would carry on." We'd put more weight on the "semi" than the "contained." CoreWeave is still the market's beta barometer for AI credit, it's the tenant on seven of the 20 project-finance data center bonds in the junk market, and the neocloud listings that tried to follow it to market keep faceplanting. Here is the latest casualty list:

Rezaei closes with what might be the most honest paragraph written about CoreWeave all month:

"We caught a lot of hate when we initiated on CRWV with a $56 price target seven months ago. Today, it's a lot harder to find bulls - certainly some of them just don't call us anymore, but there seems to be more broad acceptance of the challenges of this business model. Could this turn around? Maybe: it's a wildly volatile, momentum-driven stock, but barring major moves, the fundamentals are probably stuck."

So there you have it: one bank says CoreWeave's funding gap is $23 billion if customers prepay, GPUs last six years and the stock goes back to $64; the other says $76 billion, at 15%, for a business earning 9% (obviously, one is wrong).

Goldman's own model, meanwhile, quietly sides with the latter. Having warned since last October that AI had quietly become a debt bubble too, we know which spreadsheet we'd trust, and it's probably not the one attached to a pending underwriting. The bills, as Bernstein puts it, still have to be paid, and the first DDTL 5.0 installment comes due right about now.

Much more in the full Bernstein "Core-We've got bills to pay... lowering our PT" note and Goldman's "How big is the funding gap?", both available to pro subs.
