title: Meta Says Zuckerberg To Stay In California After Considering Relocation
desc:
Meta Says Zuckerberg To Stay In California After Considering Relocation

Authored by Zachary Stieber via The Epoch Times,

A possible new wealth tax in California prompted Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg to consider leaving the state, according to a new regulatory filing.

California voters will decide on Proposition 40 in November. It would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires.

If approved, Zuckerberg would have to pay a multibillion-dollar tax, Meta lawyers said in the Oct. 21 filing to the Securities and Exchange Commission that included frequent mentions of a special committee of independent directors.

"In light of this potential tax exposure, Mr. Zuckerberg informed the Special Committee that he was evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California and that steps toward any such relocation, including any listing of his residential real estate in California on the market, would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by Company employees and, accordingly, raise questions for management of the Company going forward," the filing stated.

The committee said Zuckerberg "has been crucial to the Company's growth since its inception," that he is best-positioned at this time to ensure the company's continued success, and that it is important to keep him in a leadership position to drive the company's continued success.

Meta, Facebook and Instagram's parent company, faced challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic, which it said stemmed from Zuckerberg's inability to be physically present with the company's management team, and the committee did not want similar challenges in the future.

The company said it is creating a new class of stock, beginning in January 2027, that will let it raise money for investment in artificial intelligence systems and incentivize Zuckerberg to remain a Meta executive.

An upcoming stock dividend will distribute class C shares to Zuckerberg and other shareholders.

"Again, the goal is to keep Mr. Zuckerberg continuing to lead the Company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs," the filing stated.

"In light of that importance, the Special Committee secured Mr. Zuckerberg's commitment to remain a resident of California, or any other jurisdiction in which the Company maintains its corporate headquarters, for eight years from the date of the Founder Alignment Agreement, for so long as Mr. Zuckerberg satisfies the Continued Leadership Condition, unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Mr. Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere."

Meta on Wednesday reported a third-quarter profit of $9.89 billion, up from $2.79 billion in the third quarter of 2025. Earnings per share were $3.83, up from $1.05.

The jump stemmed in part from much lower taxes and higher revenue.

Meta's revenue was $64.6 billion in the third quarter, and it expects to make $73 billion to $76 billion in the fourth quarter.

"We hit major milestones this quarter toward delivering personal superintelligence for everyone - including launching Muse and Muse Wonder, our first frontier model," Zuckerberg said in a statement. "Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we're seeing velocity across the board."

title: AI Discovers Critical Security Flaw Affecting Technology Behind 70% Of All Websites
desc:
AI Discovers Critical Security Flaw Affecting Technology Behind 70% Of All Websites

Artificial intelligence has uncovered a potentially catastrophic security flaw in one of the internet’s most widely used technologies, setting off a scramble among cybersecurity researchers, software developers, and website operators to prevent hackers from exploiting the discovery, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The vulnerability affects PHP, a programming technology that underpins as much as 70% of the world’s websites. Researchers discovered that weaknesses in the way PHP handles computer memory could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, potentially gaining control of websites, accessing sensitive information, and compromising visitors.

What makes the discovery particularly troubling is that the same AI technology used to identify the problem could also make it substantially easier for criminals to exploit it.

WSJ writes that the flaw, dubbed PHP2Shell, was uncovered in August by Ryan Austin of cybersecurity firm Calif, who used OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol to examine PHP’s underlying code. Although the weaknesses had been present for years, researchers had previously considered them extraordinarily difficult to exploit. With AI assistance, however, Austin demonstrated that some servers could be compromised in seconds, while more complicated systems could be breached over several hours.

The findings prompted a coordinated effort involving PHP developers, independent security researchers, and teams from Google’s Wiz and OpenAI. The group spent weeks quietly developing fixes, ultimately modifying nearly 200 files and writing more than 10,000 lines of code.

The secrecy was intentional. Researchers feared that publicizing the vulnerability before a patch was ready would give attackers an opportunity to develop their own AI-assisted exploits.

That concern reflects a broader shift in cybersecurity. Historically, hackers needed considerable time and expertise to reverse-engineer software updates and determine which weaknesses developers were attempting to correct. Advanced AI systems can now automate much of that work, potentially allowing attackers to develop working exploits before website administrators have finished installing security updates.

Volker Dusch, a security engineer associated with the nonprofit foundation responsible for PHP, called the discovery the technology’s most serious security problem in more than a decade. He compared its significance to Heartbleed, the notorious 2014 vulnerability that forced organizations around the world to urgently secure their systems.

Wiz co-founder Ami Luttwak went further, describing PHP2Shell as an exceptionally serious AI-discovered vulnerability, suggesting that its complexity might have kept it hidden indefinitely without artificial intelligence.

The developers initially targeted October 22 for releasing the patches, but details of the upcoming security update leaked onto Hacker News on Tuesday. That prompted an accelerated rollout Wednesday, as some government and commercial website operators reportedly took systems offline as a precaution and reports of attempted attacks began circulating.

The larger concern is that artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing the economics and speed of cyberattacks. The technology is allowing security researchers to uncover vulnerabilities that might otherwise remain buried for decades, while simultaneously giving malicious actors increasingly powerful tools to exploit those same weaknesses. For organizations responsible for securing the internet, the window between discovering a vulnerability and facing a potentially widespread attack may be shrinking dramatically.

title: FCC Chair Warns Broadcasters On Airing Fake Polls
desc:
FCC Chair Warns Broadcasters On Airing Fake Polls

Authored by Kimberly Hayek via The Epoch Times,

Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chairman Brendan Carr warned on Oct. 21 that broadcasters could violate their federal license obligations by airing fabricated polls or polls designed to disrupt elections and manipulate voter behavior.

Carr's statement comes just before the Nov.3 midterm congressional elections.

"During this election season, there has been a significant surge in entirely Fake Polls and Suppression Polls designed to do nothing more than interfere with the regular functioning of the electoral process and alter the normal patterns of voter turnout and enthusiasm," Carr posted on X.

He added that "many journalists and broadcasters have been amplifying or airing these Polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those Polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis."

Carr said the commission takes these issues seriously.

"Broadcasters are prohibited by the terms of their federal licenses from engaging in News Distortion or promoting Broadcast Hoaxes. It is important that broadcasters comply with their public interest obligations. After all, the country benefits greatly when Americans can trust and rely on the media to report the news fairly and accurately," he said.

He advised broadcasters "to avoid engaging in News Distortions or running Broadcast Hoaxes by airing Polls that would violate their regulatory obligations." If they believe additional context is needed for polls already covered, he said "they can now take those actions consistent with FCC regulations."

His comments came less than two weeks before the November midterm congressional elections.

Carr did not name specific polls or outlets, but one day prior, a group called Wedgewood Polling said it had fabricated data in an experiment testing media scrutiny of polling.

Wedgewood Polling said in a statement on Oct. 20 that it was developed by people who previously worked in the poll sector and wondered how easy it would be for a fabricated polling firm to gain traction, be taken seriously, and "expose how little scrutinization exists in media and public commentary."

The entity said that its surveys often did not have any real data behind them, but they were nonetheless included in poll averages by The New York Times and some other outlets.

Carr's Enforcement Approach

Carr has previously invoked the same public-interest standard when addressing broadcasters' programming.

On March 14, he threatened to strip U.S. broadcasters of their licenses over what he called false reporting on the ongoing war with Iran. "The law is clear," he said. "Broadcasters must operate in the public interest, and they will lose their licenses if they do not."

In January, Carr addressed equal-time obligations for late-night and daytime programs.

"For years, legacy TV networks assumed that their late night and daytime talk shows qualify as 'bona fide news' programs - even when motivated by purely partisan political purposes," he stated on X at the time. "Today, the FCC reminded them of their obligation to provide all candidates with equal opportunities."

Actions on Broadcast Content

Carr has also revived complaints involving election coverage and spoken about networks' responsibilities regarding programming that he said did not serve the public interest.

In January 2025, he reinstated complaints against stations affiliated with major broadcasters over their coverage of the prior presidential election.

He has stated that licensed broadcasters operate under different rules than other media because they use public airwaves.

"They have a license granted by us, the FCC, that comes with an obligation to operate in the public interest," Carr said at the time.

The FCC's authority over news content is limited. The agency states that news distortion enforcement requires deliberate distortion of a factual report, not expressions of opinion or errors from mistakes.

Zachary Stieber contributed to this report

title: Meta Ordered To Pay New Mexico $25 Billion Over Misleading Privacy Claims
desc:
Meta Ordered To Pay New Mexico $25 Billion Over Misleading Privacy Claims

Authored by Kimberly Hayek via The Epoch Times,

A Santa Fe judge on Wednesday ordered Meta Platforms to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company committed 43.9 million violations of state consumer-protection law by making misleading statements about Facebook users' data privacy and control.

The case, filed in 2021, grew out of the Cambridge Analytica scandal. New Mexico alleged that Facebook, now Meta, systematically misled the public - and New Mexico users - about how it handled personal data and allowed third-party apps access to users' information, including statements by senior executives such as CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

A jury on Sept. 25 sided with the state, finding 26 of 29 public statements by Facebook to be misleading and treating each as reaching large numbers of New Mexico Facebook users, producing a total of almost 43.9 million violations.

Under New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act, the maximum penalty is $5,000 per willful violation. Judge Francis J. Mathew of New Mexico's First Judicial District Court imposed the statutory maximum (roughly $219.5 billion) but reduced the award to $25 billion. Interest accrues at 15 percent annually until paid. Meta has said it will appeal.

"Facebook's wrongdoing - over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public - goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Mathew wrote in his order.

The jury's findings covered Facebook's statements on data practices, as well as its handling of hate speech, misinformation, and exceptions to platform rules.

"This is a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country," Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement. "A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."

Meta did not immediately return a request for comment by The Epoch Times, but its chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney, told Reuters the company is confident it will prevail on appeal.

"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico. At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney said.

In the Cambridge Analytica scandal, the now-defunct British political consulting firm obtained personal information from as many as 87 million Facebook users and used the data for political profiling and targeted advertising. New Mexico alleged that Facebook misled users about third-party access to their data and the degree of control users actually had, and that after the Cambridge Analytica event the company's statements about investigations, audits, bans, and user notifications were also misleading.

This is Meta's second major courtroom loss in New Mexico this year.

In a separate case involving the safety of young users, a jury in March imposed $375 million in civil penalties on the company. On Aug. 6, a judge ordered Meta to pay an additional $567 million into a fund for youth mental-health remedies and imposed court-supervised changes to Facebook and Instagram, bringing the total financial exposure in that case to $942 million.

US futures are lower as the AI trade discovered that there is no right answer on capex: Meta spent more, Tesla spent less, and the market slammed both (after an initial kneejerk bounce), while a fresh wave of deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia, a US-ordered departure of diplomats from the kingdom and an NYT report that the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms sent Brent back above $112; as a result the flight to quality is back on, with 10Y yields sliding 9bps to 5.03% even as oil jumps and French bond yields soar. As of 8:00am ET, S&P futures are 1.0% lower at 7,720.75 while Nasdaq futures are down 1.7% at 29,507.50 and Dow futures are 0.6% lower. Wednesday's session closed near its highs, with the S&P rising 0.6% to 7,757 for a third straight gain and closing within 1% of its record high, as the SpaceX blowout revived the AI trade. In premarket trading, all Mag 7 names are red led by Tesla, which drops 4.4% after cutting its 2026 capex target to about $20 billion from more than $25 billion, while Meta reversed an after-hours gain of as much as 5% to trade down about 1.5% as investors focused on its hedged 2027 spending commentary (as we noted last night, the stock erased most of its gains after the CFO warned "significant investment" will raise serving costs); Lam Research tumbles 8% on a soft forecast, dragging chipmakers including AMD, Broadcom and Intel. The day's driver is oil (again): Brent rose as much as 3.3% to $112.43 and WTI briefly topped $100 after two attacks on an Aramco oil field and an airport in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province killed at least three people, Aramco told staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters, and the IRGC Navy warned US bases could be targeted if Washington keeps "encouraging" ships through the Strait of Hormuz. Treasuries are bid across the curve in a bull steepener as AI doubts and another spike in French yields drive a haven bid; the OAT-Bund spread blew out by as much as 18bps to 177bps, the widest since 2011. The yen and Swiss franc lead G10 FX, with EUR/JPY at the lowest in almost a year, while the Bloomberg dollar index is little changed. Gold is down 1.3% near $4,085 and silver is down more than 3%, refusing to play haven, copper slides with the AI trade, and Bitcoin slipped below $82,000. US economic data slate includes weekly initial jobless claims (8:30am), the September leading index (10am) and the October Kansas City Fed manufacturing index (11am), and Treasury auctions resume with a $26 billion 5-year TIPS new issue (1pm). The Fed is in its blackout period ahead of next Wednesday's decision.

In premarket trading, all Mag 7 names are lower: Tesla (TSLA) drops 4.4% after the electric-car maker cut its spending plans, following capital investment that trailed expectations last quarter (Nvidia (NVDA) -2%, Alphabet (GOOGL) -2%, Amazon (AMZN) -2%, Meta Platforms (META) -2%, Microsoft (MSFT) -0.9%, Apple (AAPL) -0.2%)

  • Chipmakers and other AI-related firms slide after reports from Tesla, Lam Research and IBM underwhelmed. Decliners include AMD (AMD) -4%, Broadcom (AVGO) -3%, Intel (INTC) -4%. The mood is weighing on other growth sectors and pushing crypto names lower
  • American Airlines (AAL) slumps 4% after issuing a broad range for its fourth-quarter loss prediction, highlighting how the industry is struggling to map out its performance amid persistently high fuel prices.
  • Biohaven (BHVN) soars 53% after the FDA said company’s new drug application resubmission for Vyglxia has been accepted for review.
  • CSX (CSX) inches 2% higher after the railroad reported earnings per share for the third quarter that beat the average analyst estimate.
  • The company is benefiting as trucking gets more expensive, pushing shippers to use its intermodal offering instead of having goods carried entirely by truck.
  • Gentherm (THRM) falls 6% after the the automotive supplier reported adjusted earnings per share below analyst expectations in the third quarter.
  • International Business Machines (IBM) falls 5% after posting third quarter results.
  • Kinder Morgan (KMI) gains 2% after formally committing to building a $4.2 billion pipeline that will haul fuel across West Texas and the Panhandle to help power a data center complex.
  • Lam Research (LRCX) falls 7% after the semiconductor capital equipment company gave a forecast for adjusted second-quarter earnings that was slightly weaker than expected at the midpoint of the range.
  • Lockheed Martin (LMT) rises 4% after lifting its full-year outlook as the company’s missile systems portfolio was buoyed by rising global defense spending.
  • Pool Corp. (POOL) gains 4% after third quarter results topped expectations.
  • Procter & Gamble (PG) gains 3% after sales and profits beat Wall Street expectations, showing the Tide-owner’s limited price hikes that are successfully drawing constrained customers have not come at the expense of earnings.

In other corporate news, Meta did its best to change the subject from capex, announcing a one-time dividend of non-voting Class C shares that effectively amounts to a 2-for-1 split and, per Bloomberg, gives Mark Zuckerberg shares he can sell without giving up control as a proposed California wealth tax looms; Tesla CEO Elon Musk wants to combine Tesla and SpaceX in a $3.7 trillion deal and is rushing to get it done before Trump leaves office, according to Bloomberg; the US signed a deal with Lockheed Martin for a minimum of 850 F-35 jets; Comcast reported 3Q adjusted EPS of $1.07 vs an estimate of 98c; Blackstone's 3Q distributable income of $1.32 a share beat the $1.26 estimate; American Airlines sees a 4Q adjusted loss of 50c to $1.10 a share, vs an estimated loss of 49c; Spotify sees 4Q MAUs of 818 million, a hair below the 819.08 million estimate; Barclays is cutting 5,000 jobs, about 5% of headcount, as it adopts AI across the bank; EQT's bid for Qiagen is now firm at €46.50 a share in cash; and Chinese AI startup DeepSeek raised about 100 billion yuan ($15 billion) in its latest fundraising round.

Bloomberg sums up the overnight mood succinctly: "AI nerves are back." The bar for an AI beat has moved from ambition to monetization, and the market is no longer giving credit for spending plans alone: Meta lifted the bottom of its 2026 capex range to $135 billion from $130 billion and guided above consensus, Tesla cut its capex target after third-quarter spending came in at $4.73 billion vs $7.95 billion expected, and both stocks are lower. Spend more or spend less, the market frowned either way. IBM swung from a 5% gain to a 4.6% loss in late trading even after saying slipped infrastructure deals had come back, a reminder that software is no safe corner of the AI trade either. All of this comes as hyperscaler credit spreads sit at record wides (as we noted in last night's wrap) and as Ken Griffin calls AI "almost certainly" a bubble.

“Markets are basically telling us we are moving on from trading AI vibes and narrative to now requiring a pretty high bar for what an earnings beat looks like,” said Kaanhari Singh, APAC head of equity derivatives sales at Barclays, on Bloomberg TV. “That’s both in terms of capex forward guidance, but also for the path of monetization.”

Tesla and Lam results put “the AI confidence back in the air again, dragging a few other semi names lower,” said Anna Wu, an investment strategist and founder of Floodlines Research.

The pain was most acute in Asia, where the CSI 300 briefly entered a bear market, down 20% from its June highs, and Chinese e-commerce names including Alibaba slumped after the market regulator urged platforms to tighten product quality controls. Chinese tech stocks are now erasing most of their 2-year gain.

JPM's Market Intel desk calls it a "narrative shift overnight amid geopolitics concerns": Wednesday's session closed near its highs with AI/Tech and Momentum leading, but that tone reversed overnight. Beyond the NYT Iran headline, the desk says underlying price action and trading desk feedback point to "the still fragile narrative around AI financing concerns and the lack of conviction / re-grossing from the recent tech reversal." The team stays Tactically Bullish, favoring cyclicals outside tech while selectively buying tech weakness in semis and memory. JPM specialist Mark Schilsky called Meta's quarter in line, with a Q4 revenue guide that is "decidedly better than expected," but noted the 2027 commentary "will leave some investors wanting" and that the new Class C shares likely mean an equity raise is coming, just not until early 2027: "The overhang lives on!" Meanwhile, JPM credit trader William Jarvis notes the bank's HY AI basket is trading at all-time wides, 97bps wider than its July peak, mostly led by CoreWeave, with Oracle widening far more than the rest of IG (as Barclays warned, the AI credit flush won't be the last).

Over at Goldman, Rich Privorotsky flagged the capex whiplash: "Tesla actually cut FY capex guidance from >$25bn to ~$20bn, completely out of sync with what SpaceX was telling us earlier this week. Could be sequencing, but the market doesn't like capex going backwards." He also notes the NYT report means "we've now effectively stapled another potential escalation event to the calendar" right after the midterms, and that prime data shows one of the most pronounced net tech reductions in recent memory. The GS desk adds that hedge funds have heavily net sold global equities in October, with short sales outpacing long buys about 5 to 1, and short leverage at the 99th percentile; with positioning this defensive, the derivatives desk sees right-tail hedges as historically cheap. In Asia, Goldman's prime book shows L/S managers down 1.5% intraday and 8.6% month to date.

In Europe, the French bond rout that has carried out London macro traders deepened: France's 10Y yield hit 5.14% and its risk premium over bunds widened to 177bps, the most since 2011, as the government prepares to deploy soldiers to free up police for Saturday's protests and Paris luxury boutiques brace for more unrest. Goldman has built a fragmentation alarm to gauge how close Europe is to another "whatever it takes" moment; M&G is not worried just yet.

“We don’t believe that France needs to be bailed out. There’s no concern about this,” said M&G Asset Management CEO Joseph Pinto on Bloomberg TV. “We believe it’s a sound and solid country. It just needs to act on its budget and provide something that reassures markets.”

In Europe, the Stoxx 600 is down 0.9% at 638.75, with 445 members down and 146 up, as mixed results from US tech revive concerns about the AI trade. Miners and banks are the worst performing sectors, while telecoms, food and beverage and health care are the only gainers; JPM notes semis and electrification baskets are among the top underperformers, with only defensives and rate-sensitive baskets in the green as beta and momentum are sold. Hermès slumps after its Asia-Pacific sales disappointed, while UCB soars after raising guidance. Here are the biggest European movers:

  • Nestle gains as much as 2.7% after the company reported real internal growth for the nine month period of +1.9%, which was welcomed by analysts who noted “broad-based” improvement in RIG across different divisions and regions of the business.
  • UCB shares rally as much as 16% after the biopharma company raised its guidance, with analysts expecting material upgrades to consensus estimates.
  • Verisure shares rise as much as 17% in Stockholm after the Financial Times reported that CVC is exploring a bid to take the security group private.
  • Moncler shares rise as much as 2.8% after the Italian luxury company reported third-quarter revenue that beat consensus estimates.
  • Rentokil shares rise as much as 9.5% after the British facility management company reported revenue for the third quarter of $1.89 billion.
  • Hermès shares fall 9% after the Birkin bag maker’s third-quarter revenue fell short of analyst estimates.
  • Besi shares drop 4.3% after reporting 3Q orders that beat consensus estimates and pushing back on concerns that ASML would be a competitive threat to its flagship hybrid bonding technology.
  • Roche shares slip as much as 1.5% after the pharmaceutical firm reported third-quarter results. Analysts note the sales beat reflects a benefit from the integration of its Enterprise Resource Planning IT system.
  • SEB shared declined as much as 5.2% after the lender reported earnings that analysts say are weak and announced a pause in buybacks after Sweden’s financial regulator temporarily raised its capital requirements.
  • Yara shares fall as much as 4.7% after the fertilizer producer reported adjusted Ebitda for the third quarter that missed the average analyst estimate.
  • Sainsbury shares fall as much as 4.4% after the British supermarket reported earnings for the first half, including revenue which fell short of expectations.
  • Digital Network falls as much as 18% after the founder sold a nearly 20% stake in Polish advertising-services company through an accelerated bookbuild at a 19% discount to the previous close, upsizing the deal from an initially planned 12%.
  • Inchcape shares fall as much as 12% after the vehicle dealership group cut its margin guidance for the year due to continued underperformance of its business in Australia.
  • Nokia shares fall as much as 3%. The firm gave bullish guidance for revenues exposed to data center buildout in 2027, seeing 25% to 30% growth in optical and IP networks businesses, adding to evidence that its networking gear is seeing strong demand due to AI adoption.

Europe's Wednesday gains now look like borrowed strength: the Stoxx 600 has gone nowhere since early August while Brent and the Kospi have moved big.

Asian stocks fell sharply, with the MSCI Asia Pacific Index dropping more than 1.5% to head for its lowest close since July 30, as underwhelming US tech earnings and higher oil broadened the AI selloff across the region. According to Goldman's regional wrap, South Korea's Kospi sank 3.5% with SK Hynix down 5.5% and Samsung down 4%, the Hang Seng fell 3%, its biggest drop since March, with the Hang Seng Tech index down about 5% as Alibaba and Lenovo slumped, and the Nikkei 225 dropped 2.7% to break below 64,000 as Advantest, Tokyo Electron (-7%) and SoftBank (-6.9%) accounted for about 62% of the index's losses. China's CSI 300 fell 1.8% and is now 20% off its June high, Taiwan's Taiex lost 1.8% and Australia's ASX 200 slipped 0.4%, while Indonesia was the regional outlier, rising 1.1% as the sovereign wealth fund said it was buying local stocks. The Bank of Korea held rates at 3% but said growth would be "considerably higher" than projected, signaling more tightening to come.

In FX, the Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index is little changed and the DXY trades in a 101.44-101.73 range, pressured by lower yields. The yen is the standout, rising to its strongest against the euro in almost a year, with EUR/JPY falling as much as 1.1% to 175.64, its biggest drop in seven weeks, and USD/JPY dropping as much as 0.9% to 156.77, down for a third day; real money funds have been buying the yen, traders say, while the Swiss franc rose to its strongest against the euro since early July. Bloomberg's Vassilis Karamanis notes the dollar now trades "almost as a clean function of Treasuries: once 10-year yields slipped below 5.10%, the dollar was sold further." The kiwi lags after cooler-than-expected New Zealand CPI, the Egyptian pound hit a record low, and Turkey's central bank cut its one-week repo rate by 100bps to 36%, its first cut since the start of the Iran war and in line with estimates.

Declines in Japanese equities are fueling risk-off sentiment, while recent stability in the Japanese government bond market is also supporting the yen, Hirofumi Suzuki, chief FX strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp., told Bloomberg.

In rates, Treasury futures extend gains in early US trading with the 10-year yield down 9bps near 5.03%, outperforming global peers, as haven demand from the AI stock jitters and deepening French bond stress overwhelms higher energy prices. Yields are 6-10bps lower across the curve with intermediate tenors outperforming, richening the 2s5s30s fly by around 4bp, while the 5s30s spread is steeper by about 4bp and the 30-year yield touched its lowest since Sept. 23. The haven bid is coming from the AI selloff rather than the oil spike, and the long end is the one place investors are still finding shelter (gold and Bitcoin clearly aren't). Bunds and gilts are also bid, with the German 10-year yield down 7bps at 3.35% and long gilts outperforming, but France is the stress point: OATs fell more than a point at worst, lifting the 10-year yield to 5.14% and the spread over bunds to 177bps, the widest since 2011, while Italian and Spanish spreads also widened Wednesday. Money markets still price about 25bps of Fed hikes by year-end ahead of next Wednesday's decision, after another poor, tailing 20Y auction on Wednesday. Treasury auctions resume at 1pm with a $26 billion 5-year TIPS new issue, while the IG dollar issuance slate includes one name so far after just over $8 billion priced on Wednesday, with at least two borrowers that stood down planning to look again today.

In commodities, WTI briefly topped $100 and trades in a $97.72-$100.09 range while Brent trades between $109.81 and $112.68, still contained within Tuesday's broad range, after the IRGC Navy said four vessels transferring oil cargoes were struck in the Persian Gulf and three more hit sea mines west of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Major General Rezaei said Iran will neither reopen the strait nor resume negotiations until seven new conditions are met. Saudi Arabia is in talks to give Aramco access to foreign strategic storage, while Morgan Stanley estimates Middle East crude exports, including non-Hormuz routes, at about 17m b/d last week, roughly 94% of prewar levels. In Libya, a pipeline from the Hamada and Al-Tahara fields was shut. Spot gold sits at the bottom of its $4,067-$4,146 range as the oil spike raises inflation risks ahead of the Fed, and LME copper slid toward the bottom of its $14,090-$14,370 range on the AI selloff.

US economic data slate includes initial jobless claims (8:30am, est. 200k) and continuing claims (8:30am), the September leading index (10am), EIA natural gas storage (10:30am), the October Kansas City Fed manufacturing index (11am) and a $26 billion 5-year TIPS auction (1pm). The Fed is in its blackout period. Companies reporting before the open include Procter & Gamble, Blackstone, Union Pacific, Lockheed Martin, Honeywell, Comcast, American Airlines, Valero and Nasdaq; Valero and Bloom Energy also headline today's slate.

Market Snapshot

Top Overnight News

  • For most of the war, Iran had an invaluable cushion: dozens of oil tankers holding millions of barrels of crude sitting safely in waters in Asia. Tehran steadily sold the oil to China, bringing in billions of much-needed cash. Now, that floating storage is gone. By mid-October, the reserves were fully depleted, according to analysts at Kpler, as a U.S. naval blockade prevented Iran from replacing the crude it normally sells to Chinese refineries. WSJ
  • The US ordered some diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia because of the threat from Houthi militants, as the Iran-backed group carried out more strikes from Yemen; four people were killed in two attacks on an Aramco oil field and an airport in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. BBG
  • The US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the midterm elections, with targets likely to include Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and missile and drone arsenals. NYT
  • Aramco told staff to leave its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely. RTRS
  • Iran's IRGC threatened US bases in the region if Washington keeps escorting ships through what it calls an “illegal” Hormuz route. BBG
  • Saudi Arabia is in talks with foreign governments to give state-owned Aramco access to their strategic oil storage, as the kingdom seeks to make its supplies to customers more resilient during disruptions, Chief Executive Officer Amin Nasser said. BBG
  • The risk-off mood boosted havens, with Treasuries, the yen and Swiss franc gaining. The 30-year US yield touched its lowest since Sept. 23, but there was no relief for embattled French bonds which led a slide in European peers. BBG
  • France's 10-year bond risk premium over Germany widened as much as 18bps to 177bps, the widest since 2011. BBG
  • Over the past two weeks, HFs aggressively net sold global Info Tech stocks at the fastest pace in the past decade (-3.3 SDs), driven by long-and-short sales. Net allocation to Global AI stocks now sits in the 38th percentile while aggregate long/short ratio is in the 6th percentile vs. the past year. GSPB
  • Apple shares have become investors’ preferred Big Tech hedge against AI volatility as the company largely sits out the infrastructure spending boom. BBG
  • DeepSeek raised about $15 billion from investors including CATL and Tencent. BBG
  • JPM's HY AI credit basket is trading at all-time wides, 97bps wider than its widest level in July, with most of the move led by CoreWeave; Oracle has widened far more than the rest of the IG hyperscalers. JPM
  • Japan’s largest labor union group is seeking another year of wage increases big enough to anchor pay growth against persistent inflation. WSJ
  • Japanese monetary policy: the BOJ will keep rates unchanged at its meeting next week according to a report this morning in the Nikkei (this is consistent w/market expectations). Nikkei
  • The Philippine central bank surprised markets with a bigger-than-expected interest rate hike as it seeks to keep inflation in check during one of the worst energy crisis in decades and looming weather-driven shocks. WSJ
  • Turkey's central bank cut its one-week repo rate by 100bps to 36%, its first cut since the start of the Iran war, in line with estimates. BBG
  • The EU reached a provisional deal to overhaul securitization market rules that would unleash billions of euros to finance initiatives in key areas such as defense and climate resilience. BBG
  • Barclays said it’s cutting 5,000 jobs, or about 5% of total headcount, as part of a “technology-enabled” effort to reduce costs as it adopts artificial intelligence across the bank. BBG
  • The US signed a deal with Lockheed Martin for a minimum of 850 F-35 jets. BBG
  • A federal judge barred the DHS from knocking on doors to check on people’s immigration status in nine states through election day, saying the practice likely violates the Voting Rights Act. BBG
  • BofA Total Card Spending (week to October 17th) +4.9% Y/Y (prev. +5.1%); lower-income spending growth has consistently outpaced higher-income spending growth over the past several weeks. Newsquawk
  • Some US banks are reportedly detecting unauthorised AI agents operating within accounts: Axios. The report added that the banks affected include Morgan Stanley (MS), Bank of America (BAC), JPMorgan (JPM), Wells Fargo (WFC).

A more detailed look at global markets courtesy of Newsquawk

APAC stocks were pressured and extended on losses throughout the session despite the positive lead from Wall Street, as AI and semiconductor names were sold after Tesla cut capex guidance, Lam Research fell after-hours, and Meta's results stoked concerns over the financial strain of heavy AI investment. Middle East tensions also remained in focus, with the US preparing ordered departures at embassies across the Gulf and reports of renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia. ASX 200 was lower, with energy and retail stocks leading the declines as Nick Scali slumped after its profit warning and weighed on fellow retailers, although the index pared some of its earlier losses. Nikkei 225 extended on losses, with AI and semiconductor names such as Tokyo Electron, SoftBank Group, Ibiden and Fujikura pressured. KOSPI underperformed as concerns over investment in the AI value chain sparked a selloff in chip stocks, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both pressured, while Samsung Electro-Mechanics reversed the opening gains it saw on its NVIDIA tie-up. The BoK held rates unanimously, as expected, while Governor Shin said the recent stock market correction weighs on consumption. Hang Seng led the declines in the region with Lenovo and Hua Hong Semiconductor each down around 7% and CATL extending its losing streak to a seventh day, while the Shanghai Comp declined amid uncertainty over the Middle East, with semiconductor names sold.

Top Asian News

  • BoJ's October lending survey: Corporate loan demand DI rose to +3 (prev. -1), led by small firms (+5), while banks' lending stance DI for large firms remained unchanged at +3 and corporate loan margins continued to narrow.
  • Japan's RENGO set 2027 wage negotiation target centred on a 6% pay increase, while maintaining a minimum benchmark of at least 5%, aiming to sustain wage growth momentum following three consecutive years of average pay rises exceeding 5%.
  • Japan is reportedly considering broadening the definition of defence-related spending to include AI, satellites, R&D and infrastructure such as ports and railways, amid US pressure to increase defence outlays and domestic fiscal constraints, according to sources.

European bourses are under pressure this morning, following on from the weakness seen in Asia. In Hong Kong, the likes of Alibaba (-6.1%) and PDD (-3.6%) slipped after China’s CMRC urged e-commerce platforms to strengthen product quality controls and consumer protection. Sectors highlight the negative bias. Telecoms, Food, Beverages & Tobacco and Health Care are the sector gainers. The underperformer is Basic Resources, followed by Banks and Tech. Key earnings include: SAP -0.9%, despite Q3 metric beats and sees FY26 cloud revenue at the upper end of its guided range; Nestle +1.6%, Q3 sales beat and reaffirms its FY26 sales growth target; Roche -0.5%, despite Q3 sales topping estimates and reaffirms FY outlook; Nokia -5.3%, despite Q3 profit beating expectations and expects supply chain constraints to continue in 2027. US equity futures follow the broader space lower, with underperformance in the NQ, pressured by Tesla (-4.5% pre-market) after reporting slower deliveries growth. Meta (-1.2% pre-market) follows sentiment lower, despite reporting strong Q3 results, but with potential focus on the Co. being ordered to pay a USD 25bln penalty to New Mexico.

FX

  • G10s are mixed against the USD. JPY is the clear outperformer, joined closely by the CHF, benefiting from haven flows. On the flip side, the Antipodeans have been hampered by the risk tone, whilst the Kiwi digests cooler-than-expected CPI.
  • DXY is on the back foot this morning, pressured by lower yields, which comes despite elevated energy prices. The index currently holds at the upper end of a 101.44 to 101.73 range; price action today will likely be dictated by cross-asset relationships, given that the data docket remains light today. Some of the pressure today may also be facilitated by poor results from Tesla.
  • The JPY is the outperformer this morning, benefiting from its safe haven status. USD/JPY currently holds at the bottom end of a 156.76 to 158.25 range, a move which will no doubt be welcomed by Japanese officials. Focus for geopolitics was on an IRGC warning to US bases, that they may be a target if the US continues to allow ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. Aside from geopolitics, the JPY is digesting reports that Japan is considering the resumption of energy subsidies. Whilst this does reduce the inflationary implications of recent energy price rises, the overarching question is how Japan intends to finance this; of course, options include a supplementary budget, which could involve bond issuance, further fuelling fiscal woes. Elsewhere in Japan, the RENGO union is reportedly seeking a 6% wage increase for 2027, an increase from the 2026 figure of 5.01%; for reference, the union had demanded 5.94% in 2026.
  • The Antipodeans are the slight laggards this morning, given the subdued risk tone. The Kiwi mildly underperforms vs the Aussie following a cooler-than-expected CPI report, but still remains at elevated levels. Therefore, money markets still expect the RBNZ to hike rates at next week’s meeting; Westpac sees rates to be hiked by 25bps.

Central Banks

  • BoK left its rate unchanged at 3.0% as expected. BoK said today's rate decision was unanimous, while the timing and pace of further rate hikes will depend on inflation, economic conditions and financial stability. It is essential to assess domestic and external risks and the impact of the previous two rate hikes. Expects inflation to remain above its target for an extended period. Stock price volatility has increased amid concerns over slowing semiconductor sector profitability and investment. Financial imbalances related to the housing market and household debt require continued attention. Expects exports and investment to sustain strong growth.
  • SNB Minutes (Sept): The rise in inflation since the beginning of the year has been largely attributable to the increase in oil product prices, but there are still no signs of second-round effects, and core inflation has risen only slightly. At the same time, medium-term inflationary pressure is only slightly higher, and the new conditional inflation forecast shows that inflation is within the range consistent with price stability over the entire forecast horizon. On FX, the Minutes state that the SNB is also willing to be active in the foreign exchange market as necessary to ensure appropriate monetary conditions, but that the increased willingness to intervene is no longer necessary in the current environment.

Fixed Income

  • In brief, a haven bid is seen across most core fixed income, as the geopolitical situation escalates and yields prove somewhat resilient to the energy upside, as much of that is priced by this stage, with focus instead increasingly on the growth side of the equation.
  • USTs just off a 105-19+ peak, firmer by 16 ticks at best. The docket ahead is relatively light, but the focus is firmly on geopolitics after the activity seen in APAC hours and the continued dissemination of punchy rhetoric in the European morning.
  • Bunds also bid, and in-fitting with USTs for the most part. At a 121.90 high, firmer by 50 ticks. As above, specifics are relatively light and the focus is firmly on geopolitical developments for core counterparts.
  • In brief, while the focus for core debt is increasingly on the growth implications of the ongoing Middle East situation, this is not to a degree that is likely to dissuade policymakers from tightening in the weeks ahead, with the BoE for instance expected to start its tightening cycle; though, it is expected to be brief.
  • Continuing with the UK, Gilts opened with modest gains, given the above haven allure factoring initially, before then being briefly unwound/offset by energy’s influence. However, Gilts broadly conform to peers, with gains of around 15 ticks currently, some 10 off the 84.73 peak.
  • More pertinently, those under significant fiscal scrutiny are seeing a selloff as the growth-hit and inflationary angle combine to further knock the fiscal backdrop. A point that is particularly evident in France, with OATs down by over a point at most, lifting the 10yr yield to a 5.14% high, and widening the OAT-Bund spread to 1.73%, the highest since January 2011.
  • The UK sells GBP 1bln 0.125% 2031 I/L Gilt: b/c 3.99x (prev. 4.26x), real yield 1.141% (prev. 0.933%).

Commodities

  • Crude benchmarks have climbed throughout the APAC session and continue as Europe steps in. Iran’s IRGC Navy said four vessels transferring oil cargoes were struck in the Persian Gulf, while three other vessels hit sea mines yesterday west of the Strait of Hormuz, warning that US efforts to encourage passage could result in strikes on US bases. With repeated airing of these comments, it has continued to support the energy complex. WTI briefly topped USD 100/bbl, but currently holds at the upper end of its USD 97.72-100.09/bbl range, while Brent trades in a USD 109.81-112.68/bbl range. All being said, the crude complex remains contained within Tuesday’s broad range.
  • Elsewhere, the NYT reported that the US and Israeli militaries have developed plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections, targeting energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and missile and drone arsenals, while Israeli press cited US official comments that there has apparently been a change in the American position in favour of a pre-emptive strike on Iran.
  • Spot gold has come under pressure in the European morning, as it resides at the lower end of its USD 4067-4146/oz range. Zooming out to the range formed over the past month, the yellow metal sits at the bottom of that range (USD 4066-4228/oz). The precious metal has not been favoured by usual risk-off flows or a weaker dollar, but instead found headwinds from escalating Middle East hostilities, which have raised inflation risks ahead of the Fed decision next week.
  • 3M LME Copper slid overnight and currently holds at the bottom end of its USD 14.09k-14.37k/t range. The red metal is tracking the losses in the equity space, over continued worries of the AI trade. Copper has benefited recently due to its use in data centres and power infrastructure.
  • US waived Russian diesel tax record requirements for buyers.

title: Music Publishers Sue Anthropic For Copyright Infringement
desc:
Music Publishers Sue Anthropic For Copyright Infringement

Authored by Stacy Robinson via The Epoch Times,

A federal district court in California is set to hear arguments this week as a group of music publishers sues Anthropic, alleging that the artificial intelligence (AI) firm is stealing their work.

Led by Concord Music Group, the plaintiffs say that Anthropic trained its AI model, Claude, using copyrighted lyrics from their artists. The next hearing is slated for Oct. 21.

In a separate case, Concord alleges that Anthropic used pirated copies of 20,517 music works - accessed from torrent sites - to train Claude.

The lawsuits are just two of dozens of legal actions taken by publishers in the book, news, and art industries, as creatives argue that AI companies have trained their models on existing work with an intent to replace human ingenuity with machine outputs.

When prompted, Claude will create a new set of song lyrics that are similar to existing work, Concord says, or generate a new song using similar chord progressions.

"For example, when asked by Publishers' investigator to write "a song about the death of Buddy Holly," Claude generated a verbatim copy of the lyrics to 'American Pie,'" a court filing says.

The Claude AI tool will also spit out lyrics to copyrighted songs upon request, and Concord argues that this cuts into its profits.

If a web user wants to know the words to "Uptown Funk" or "Hey Jude," a simple Google search will bring up any number of websites containing the lyrics. But those websites pay a licensing fee to republish the lyrics. Getting the song texts for free through AI makes those websites obsolete, Concord argues, and deprives the publishers of that extra revenue.

For its part, Anthropic is arguing that the Fair Use doctrine allows it to use the song lyrics. That legal principle allows use of copyrighted work under certain circumstances, such as teaching or criticism, or when the copyrighted material is substantially transformed into something new.

Anthropic recently had to settle a case for $1.5 billion after a group of book publishers sued. It used the same fair use argument, but only with partial success.

Although the judge in that case agreed that using copyrighted material to train AI models was fair use, the company had initially used pirated versions of the books taken from the internet. That may end up being relevant for Concord's second lawsuit.

Anthropic also said that Claude contains "copyright-protective" features and that it isn't the company's fault when a user finds a workaround.

"When a system 'creates the copy only in response to the user's command,' its operator does not engage in volitional conduct," Anthropic said in a court filing. "The user does."

Concord is asking the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California in San Jose to award up to $150,000 per copyright violation, along with another $25,000 for instances where it alleges that Claude removed copyright notices from song lyrics. Or else, it at least wants the profits it lost by the infringement - an undisclosed amount Concord said it will later document in court.

At the end of last month, the plaintiffs submitted a short brief noting a recent appeals court decision they hope will galvanize their cases.

On Sep. 30, the Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled against the fair use argument in a similar case where Thomson Reuters sued AI company ROSS Intelligence.

Reuters developed a legal research database called Westlaw, and the entries contain "headnotes," which are short, hand-crafted annotations that summarize the information. According to a court filing, ROSS hired an outside company to provide material to train its AI tool, and that company used 25,000 Westlaw headnotes for that purpose.

In ruling for Reuters, the Third Circuit said that this was not fair use, partly because the ROSS tool was specifically created to be a competitor to Westlaw.

However, California is covered by the Ninth Circuit, so the court won't be strictly bound by that precedent when it considers the Anthropic lawsuit.

UBS macro strategist Simon Penn wrote in a note to clients that the surge in French yields and the widening spread were due to "budget rejections."

Penn added more color:

The French 10-year yield has opened Thursday higher, at 5.05%, up 3.6bp on the day so far. That's pushed the spread to Germany out another 5.5bp.

The news flow has moved away from street protests and back to the roots of the budget. The government isn't finding any takers for its budget proposals so far. The bond market is hence reacting accordingly. The next threat comes later Thursday afternoon if MPs indicate today's proposals to cut spending are also to be rejected.

title: Ken Griffin Says AI Is "Almost Certainly" A Bubble As Corporate America Opens Its Anthropic And OpenAI Bills
desc:
Ken Griffin Says AI Is "Almost Certainly" A Bubble As Corporate America Opens Its Anthropic And OpenAI Bills

The man who runs one of the world's most profitable hedge funds and America's biggest market maker has a word for the AI trade, and it starts with a "b".

Speaking at the Future of Global Markets Conference in New York on Tuesday, Citadel founder Ken Griffin told Bloomberg that investors are "almost certainly" in the midst of an artificial intelligence bubble, as many companies are still figuring out how much they will spend on the technology and what, exactly, they are getting for it.

"Corporate America has been very uneven in its ability to extract value from its AI models. I think all of Corporate America is looking at their bills from Anthropic and OpenAI and going, 'Okay, we need to think about how to make sure we're getting productivity out of this.'"

That could be a problem because as BCA Research showed this week, so far AI has not produced an economy-wide acceleration in productivity growth. In fact, adjusted for shifts in utilization rates, total factor productivity growth was zero in Q2. Said otherwise, there has been zero productivity boost from AI!

And just in case anyone thought that was a throwaway line:

"Any radical transformation of our economy is generally intertwined with a bubble. These bubbles, if we want to use that word, often coincide with these giant technological transformations."

In other words, the best-paid man in the room thinks the room is in a bubble, and he is fine saying so out loud. Which, for regular readers, will sound familiar: we have been warning since last October that the AI boom runs on debt, and lately the market has started doing the warning for us.

To be sure, nobody will care this is a bubble... until the market crashes, at which point everyone will scream how nobody warned them in advance. And just like that the new TBTF is born.

"Looking At Their Bills"

Griffin's timing was impeccable, maybe a little too impeccable. Hours earlier, the WSJ reviewed a fresh draft of Anthropic's S-1, which we broke down in "Anthropic's Updated S-1: An $80.7BN Half-Year Loss, A $750BN Compute-Tab, And A 'Catastrophic Incident' Warning." The short version: Anthropic booked $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, posted an $80.7 billion GAAP net loss (about $72 billion of which is a non-cash revaluation of financing instruments, leaving a still-hefty ~$8.7 billion underlying loss), and has signed more than $600 billion of mostly noncancelable compute contracts, with talks under way for another $150 billion. That would take the tab to as much as $750 billion.

Our reaction to the revenue headline was, well, brief:

*ANTHROPIC HAD $16.3B IN REVENUE IN FIRST HALF OF 2026: WSJ that's it?

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 20, 2026

Here is what that looks like on one chart: eventually someone has to pay for the blue bars, and Griffin just told us the customers are starting to check the invoices.

Griffin, for his part, said Anthropic's success will ultimately depend on proving to investors that its models are a must-have across every industry. That is a tall order when the price of the product keeps falling (and that ignores the fact that as "every industry" finds models are indispensably, it fires "almost every" worker currently employed, leading to a labor depression) . As we showed last week, Anthropic's token prices have tumbled to an all-time low:

Falling prices and decelerating growth are a tricky combination for a company with fixed, ten-year take-or-pay obligations. It is also why IPO investors marked the valuation down to $1.5 trillion last week after Anthropic's Q3 numbers showed the sequential growth rate hitting the brakes. Put differently, the bill keeps rising and the price per unit keeps falling, and the gap is what the IPO is supposed to fund.

From "Garbage" To "Depressed" To "Golden Era"

To be fair to Griffin, his AI views have had quite a year. Speaking in Davos in January, he called AI garbage, per Bloomberg. By May he told an audience at Stanford Business School that he was depressed by everything AI could achieve. On Tuesday he struck a sunnier tone, arguing the technology will unleash a wave of new business formation in the US:

"You're seeing the threat to white collar jobs playing out; as a business owner, you're seeing your competitive moats be filled in by bulldozers. At the same time, you're thinking that this will be a golden era for entrepreneurs."

Garbage, then depressing, then a golden era that happens to be a bubble. Three views in ten months is roughly how the market has traded AI too, so maybe he is just being consistent.

Griffin also pointed back to the days before the dot-com crash and some of the "fanciful" business models of that era:

"The companies that are on the other side of that bubble are the market leaders for decades to come. I just wish I'd kept my Amazon stock in that moment."

A fair point, with one footnote: anyone who kept their Amazon stock through that moment first had to sit through a drawdown of more than 90%. The winners on the other side of a bubble tend to get there the hard way.

Goldman: Breadth Is At Its Narrowest Since The Dot-Com Bubble

Griffin isn't the only one reaching for the 2000 analogy. Goldman's chief US equity strategist Ben Snider, in his latest US Weekly Kickstart (available to pro subs), notes that with the S&P 500 just 2% from its record high but the median S&P 500 stock 15% from its high, Goldman's preferred measure of breadth "remains near its narrowest level since the Dot-Com Bubble."

Snider also tackles the "productivity" question Griffin raised, from the earnings side. He expects S&P 500 EPS growth to slow from 29% in 2026 to 18% in 2027 (adjusting for accounting distortions), and warns that "slowing AI investment growth will be a fading tailwind." How big a tailwind? Goldman's Asia sales desk (Dani Wojdyla) puts it bluntly in this week's "Positioning Reset" note: "AI capex is currently contributing about half of S&P 500 EPS growth," an impulse Goldman expects "to diminish as capex growth slows and depreciation builds."

Translation: half of the earnings growth the market is paying for comes from companies spending money on AI, which shows up as someone else's revenue... and eventually as everyone's depreciation. The early Q3 read already shows the slope turning: 53% of S&P firms have beaten consensus EPS so far, above the 25-year average of 50% but well below the 64% rate of the past four quarters.

Last week Goldman's Tony Pasquariello argued breadth "isn't so bad"... then brought up the dot-com bubble twice, including a 2027 supply wildcard that could lift net US equity supply by the most since 2000. Anthropic's IPO, of course, is a big chunk of that wildcard.

Over at BofA, Michael Hartnett's team has done the bubble math on concentration. Peak concentration in the major bubbles of the past two centuries clustered around 40% (railroads were the outlier at 63%). The "AI Big 10" (Mag 7 plus Broadcom, AMD and Micron) recently hit 42%, above the 41% TMT peak in 2000:

Nothing says "healthy market" like a chart where the current reading sits between the Nifty Fifty and Japan in 1989.

Credit Got There First

If equity investors are only now discovering the word "bubble", the credit market has been pricing it for weeks. Per Goldman credit strategist Amanda Lynam's Global Credit Trader, "AI, Credit, and a Higher Cost of Capital" (also available to pro subs), USD HY AI-related spreads widened 25bp to 360bp over Treasuries, compared with just 2bp for non-AI issuers, with data center issuers leading the way:

Even Goldman's strategists, who just moved tactically overweight equities in their latest GOAL Kickstart, concede the point in the same note:

"Concerns on AI capex returns and funding are increasingly showing up in credit: CCC-BB spreads, hyperscaler CDS and neocloud OAS have all widened, with the latest move particularly sharp for neocloud issuers."

So Goldman is long the stocks and short the credit, while the credit is the one sending the warning. Their own Risk Appetite Indicator just "turned negative for the first time since March 2026," with all five sub-components down over the past month. Bullish, maybe... but not exactly confident.

The equity-credit gap is stark. As Goldman's basket desk showed in a chart we highlighted in "Trick Or Treat", hyperscaler equities were about 15% lower the last time hyperscaler credit spreads were this wide:

And the debt pile is only getting bigger. Goldman's credit team expects project finance plus direct hyperscaler issuance to hit $720 billion in 2027, up from $37 billion of project finance in all of 2025, with risks "firmly skewed to the upside":

The cracks are already showing where capital meets reality. Korea's Elice cratered 32% on its debut despite a retail tranche 400 times oversubscribed, and Australia's Nextdc imploded 45% and is mulling force majeure as protesters stall power to its Melbourne campus. Fink: The Bubble Can't Stop Inflating

Not everyone in the C-suite agrees with Griffin, or rather they agree, they just don't see any way out. Less than a day after the Citadel CEO's comments, BlackRock's Larry Fink took the opposite side, warning on Bloomberg TV from the Berlin Global Dialogue that the real danger is building too slowly. Per Bloomberg:

"If we don't build out these data centers, it is actually more inflationary because the cost of compute is so high right now. And the faster we can build out more data centers, the more compute we have, the faster we can bring down the cost."

Incidentally, this is precisely the point we made a month ago:

The more data centers are lit, the faster this bubble pops

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) September 25, 2026

And, just to raise the stakes, Fink added that "If we slow down the build out of this technology, I think it really does jeopardize the economy." (Deutsche Bank's Christian Sewing, for what it's worth, also played down Griffin's bubble fears on Wednesday.)

Translation: the bubble is too important to stop inflating. Coming from the head of a firm whose infrastructure arm is among the biggest data center buyers on the planet, maybe that is not a huge surprise.

Fink does have a point on the physical bottleneck, and it is one we have been hammering for months: the constraint is power, permits and angry neighbors, which is why we keep arguing that "behind the meter" generation should be mandatory for new campuses. Nextdc's Melbourne fiasco is exactly that constraint in action, and so are the billions in Nvidia chips collecting dust in Amazon warehouses because there is nowhere to plug them in.

But the rest of his argument runs into the numbers above. If compute is so scarce and expensive, it is odd that Anthropic's token prices just hit an all-time low and its revenue growth is slowing (thank Chinese open-source models, which Dario is desperate to ban at the sovereign level). More importantly, building faster means borrowing faster, and Fink himself flagged the problem in the same interview:

"We're at a time now where we're finally unlocking private capital, and so the competition for capital is as large as I've ever seen in my professional career."

He also said bond yields are "flashing," adding: "Wake up, federal government. Our deficits are starting to have real large issues." Put the two together and you get the trade-off we have been describing for months: every extra dollar of AI debt is competing with Uncle Sam's ~$2 trillion deficit for the same duration buyers, with the 10Y already above 5%. As we noted on Sept 1, AI issuance has been crowding out Treasuries. In other words, Fink's cure for compute inflation (build more, faster, with borrowed money) is a fine recipe for bond-market inflation.

Who Holds The Bag On The Other Side?

Griffin's bubble call comes with a familiar bullish escape hatch: bubbles fund revolutions, and the survivors become the Amazons of the next two decades. That is probably right about the technology. It says very little about the price anyone pays to get there, or about who ends up holding the paper when the bills come due.

Griffin says it's a bubble; Fink says stopping it would be inflationary. Both can be right, which is precisely the problem. And right now the bills are piling up on both sides. On one side, Anthropic needs public investors to backstop as much as $750 billion of compute it has already promised to pay for. On the other, its biggest customers (per Griffin) are starting to ask what they are getting for their money. Meanwhile half of S&P earnings growth depends on the capex continuing, the credit market is already charging more to fund it, and the bond market (per Fink himself) is "flashing."

So we'll side with Griffin's first word over his last one. The AI buildout will probably produce a few generational winners, but the path from here to there looks a lot more like 2000-2002 than like a "golden era", and as usual, credit is telling equities which way the bubble deflates. If the man with the best seat in the house wishes he had kept his Amazon shares, maybe the more useful lesson is that he didn't buy more of them in March 2000.
